Their keys were published in 2017; the messages fail because letters were lost or added in transmission. The known keys were applied with a search for up to two garbled blocks per message. Nine had been decrypted in the 2017 comment thread and three in part; the search reproduces those. A September 2026 decipherment of page 217 was verified here against the ciphertext, and the other nine give nothing under any known key. Lasry’s 2017 attack broke 618 cryptograms under fourteen keys; 22 messages did not decrypt and were published as an unsolved list. The cipher ADFGVX with a columnar transposition. One lost or added letter moves every column boundary after it, so a garbled message fails even under the right key. How it was tried The 2017 comment-thread decryptions are gathered in one table. Norbert’s method (two block edits of up to five letters against a known key) is reimplemented with a German language model and re-derives the solved pages without their plaintext. What was added The list should read “22 messages, 9 decrypted, 3 partly decrypted, 10 open”, and the key Lasry recovered in the thread belongs with the published fourteen. Still open The ten open messages: no result with any of the fifteen keys, and a key-free attack cannot recover the transposition at these lengths, even on a planted control. They need the Childs originals or a key not in the corpus. Credit Lasry, Niebel, Kopal and Wacker (2017); Norbert Biermann, Armin, Thomas, Max Baertl and Lasry in the thread.
adfgvx.html#list

James Rives Childs, the American cryptanalyst attached to the French in 1918, kept a transcript of German ADFGVX traffic intercepted on the Eastern Front. In 2017 George Lasry, Ingo Niebel, Nils Kopal and Arno Wacker broke the corpus with a hill-climbing attack on the transposition and recovered 618 cryptograms under fourteen three-day keys, from September to December 1918. Lasry then gave Klaus Schmeh a list of the messages that would not decrypt under any of those keys, and Schmeh published it as “Unsolved ADFGVX messages from World War I”, with the keys attached, and later as no. 46 on his Top 50. Lasry’s own note on that page says what the problem is: the keys are “most certainly all the keys used during the period”, so “the challenge is to understand how the cryptograms were mutilated”. ADFGVX is unforgiving about length. The columnar transposition splits the letter stream by the key length, so one lost or added letter moves every column boundary after it and turns the rest of the message into noise. A message with two garbles is no longer decryptable by the key, even though the key is known. Between February and September 2017 the comment thread under the post did most of the work. Norbert Biermann, Armin, Thomas, Max Baertl and Lasry himself decrypted message after message. Schmeh announced a consolidating article and never wrote it, so those decryptions existed only as scattered comments, and no table of the results was found in print or online. The first thing this write-up does is publish that table.
adfgvx.html#keys

Lasry’s list gives each key as a transposition permutation and a 36-character substitution square, the cells in row order of A D F G V X. Three of the fourteen squares contain runs of hyphens for cells never recovered, and the text layer of the PDF collapses those runs into en- and em-dashes, leaving squares of 34 or 35 characters. Expanding each dash back to the run length that makes 36 repairs all three. All fourteen are in keys.json . The key numbers admit two interpretations. Either perm[i] is the column emitted i-th, or it is the position at which column i is emitted. Both round-trip self-consistently, so an encrypt-decrypt test cannot tell them apart. Decrypting a real message can. It is the second. The key not on the list On 3 May 2017 Lasry reported in the thread that a two-part message, the FFVXV cryptogram of 13 November and the AFAFF fragment that continues it, decrypted jointly under a key that was in none of the fourteen periods: transposition word CMBLAKOHIDENFJGP, length 16. He gave the joint plaintext, 173 letters, and noted that his program had needed all 356 ciphertext letters to recover a length-16 key. The substitution square was not published. It is rebuilt here by aligning the untransposed bigrams of the two cryptograms with his plaintext, Norbert’s corrections applied: 24 of 36 cells, with the digits and the letters M, Q and Y unrecovered because the message never uses them. It is the fifteenth entry in keys.json and the repo’s notes call it the CHI key, after the header of the message it enciphered.

Page 217 was not decrypted in 2017. On 17 September 2026 “prinz” posted its decipherment under the transposition keyword TRUPPENVERSCHIEBUNG, a key Childs lists (pp. 214–215) for use from 9 December (reported by The Neuron, 18 September 2026). It was checked here as known plaintext: under that transposition the 170 received letters give 85 pairs, and the 85 letters of the reported text map onto them one to one (23 distinct pairs, 23 distinct letters, no conflict); the 23 recovered cells fall into a keyword-shaped square (T R U P E 4 / N · S C 2 H). The message says that a British cruiser has come into Sevastopol on the 24th and an Allied squadron follows on the 26th. The same key gives noise on the nine other open messages. Max Baertl’s 2017 text of VGADA (p. 215) was checked letter by letter against the cells: 97 of its 129 letters are carried, but 20 contradict the received cells, so it stays a partial decryption. One further transcript page, 187 as printed (SELLV…, “Stellv. Gen. Kom. 9 AK Breslau”), was a message the Kassel team had already solved and does not belong on the list; Lasry said so in the thread. The two CHI messages were listed as undecryptable under the published keys, which is true; they were decrypted after Lasry recovered a key that was not published.

adfgvx.html#method

Norbert stated his method in one sentence: add or remove up to five characters at two different positions, exhaustive search, an n-gram value function to rank the results. blocks.py does exactly that. For each of the fifteen keys, and each choice of up to two block edits of one to five letters, inserted or deleted at the five-letter group boundaries of the transcript, it decrypts and scores the result with a German quadgram model built from 3.6 million letters of Gutenberg German ( lm_de.py ). Windows that contain a digit or an unrecovered cell cost a floor; windows that cross an X separator cost less than junk and more than text. German prose scores about −3.3 nats per window on this model, and random letters about −7. Given no hint of the plaintext, the search re-derives pages 105, 109, 146 and 171, the “missing 10 letters” message of page 176, and the two CHI messages. On page 146 the five-letter block that Norbert inserted before group 10 comes out as (45, 5) . On the page-176 message the two five-letter blocks come out as (10, 5), (130, 5) . Page 100 falls to the same search with one two-letter insertion. The search also finds the Nov 22–24 partial of the unnumbered VGADA message. Where the printed transcription marks gaps, gaps.py restores them to their groups and anneals the residual single-letter losses; on page 132 it lands on Norbert’s text unprompted. The scores of the re-derived pages, from the run log, against the best any of the open messages achieves: page key length best score, nats per window decrypt as returned by the search 187 (CHI part 1) 16 −4.45 RUSSISCHETUNDPOLNHEERESVERKEHRVOLLERFASSENXWICHTIGESBESONDERS… 146 17 −5.25 FUNKSTELLEKERTSCHERHAE.TAB12X1.XRUFNAME.RICHARD.MILKARLX… AFAFF (CHI part 2) 16 −5.28 SOWEITFERNSCHREIBERVERBDGNITHTARBEICETXRESTSCHRIFTLICHXNACHCHEF… 100 19 −5.39 KEI.ESTOERFNGDURCHFEINDXMITTAGS2FEINDLXDIVXIMMARSCHAUFBELGRAD. 171 20 −5.50 INUKRAI.EUNDPOLEN.UBELKURSETARKSIEIGENDINFOLGEBRUCHEEZWISCHEN… 105 19 −6.02 GERMANIAATAPPEKONSTANTINOPELX6FUERMITTJLMEERDIVISIVNZUXTELXNRX62… 109 19 −6.02 OXFXMXABECDMELUNGXS4VCXUMBJRGABGLETZTEVTEILEBEEVUKTX1WEITEDE… best open message (158, 170) 20, 19 −6.89 noise The solved pages are recognisable German at a glance even where the block edit is not quite right, and the residual garbles are the single-letter losses that a second pass repairs. The 105 and 109 lines score lower than the others because the two-block search only approximates their mutilation; both texts are nevertheless legible in the raw output and both agree with Norbert’s 2017 decryptions.

The solved messages come out between −4.4 and −6.0 on the same run, and random letters at about −7.3. So none of the ten is one of the fifteen keys with two or fewer block mutilations, which is exactly the boundary the 2017 readers reached and stopped at. A digit-heavy output is the usual sign of a wrong key: real traffic here is mostly letters, and a wrong square scatters bigrams across the digit cells. The CHI key on the two page-153 messages In September 2017 Norbert suggested, without testing it, that the two page-153 messages might belong to the CHI key, since they are of the same period. Direct decryption with parity repair, and the block search, both return noise for both messages. The cause is a further unlisted key or losses heavier than two blocks. A key-free attack, and why it fails If some of the open messages were enciphered under a key not in the corpus, the key would have to be recovered from the ciphertext alone. keyless.py tries: anneal the column order at each candidate length on the index of coincidence of the letter pairs the untransposition produces, since a correct untransposition pairs the bigrams of a monoalphabetic substitution, then solve the 36-symbol substitution with the German model. Before running it on the open messages it was run on a planted control: 224 letters of German enciphered under a length-19 key of the same design. candidate length 15 16 17 18 19 (true) 20 21 22 23 pair IC after annealing 0.055 0.048 0.060 0.053 0.064 0.058 0.066 0.063 0.073 The true length does not stand out: the peak at 19 is beaten by 21, 22 and 23, and the substitution stage does not converge at any length. The control is not recovered . Lasry’s own program, built for this purpose, needed 356 letters to recover a length-16 key. The nine open messages are 84 to 240 letters long. A key-free recovery is therefore out of reach at these lengths, with one exception: two or more open messages that share an unknown key could be solved jointly, as the two CHI messages were. Nothing in the ciphertext marks which those would be, and the two page-153 messages, the natural candidates, give nothing when tried together.
adfgvx.html#status

Ten messages are decrypted, three in part, nine open. The open messages were tested in September 2026 and fail under every known key with up to two block edits; page 217, open then, was deciphered under a further key that same month (section 03), and that key fails on the other nine too. Three things would change that. what why it would matter The Childs originals Several of the nine carry explicit gap marks in the printed transcription and one is labelled “missing 10 letters”. The transcription Schmeh printed is a copy of a copy; the intercept sheets may hold the letters the search has to guess. A further key The CHI message proved the published list is not complete. A key recovered from any other source, or from a longer message in the same period that was never on this list, could be tested against all ten in seconds. A search past two edits Three block edits against fifteen keys is within reach of compute and is the natural next step; it was not run here because two edits was the standard that solved everything the 2017 readers solved, and the scores give no sign that any open message is close. Until one of those arrives, the useful products are the table above, the fifteen keys in machine-readable form with the three damaged squares repaired and the CHI square rebuilt, and a decoder that reproduces the 2017 decryptions without being given their plaintext.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. 22 ADFGVX messages, Childs pages 73-217 (Nov 1918): the nine read in full (pp. 100, 105, 109, 132, 146, 171, 176, 187 part 1 and its part 2 AFAFF) German ADFGVX radio messages of November 1918 from James Rives Childs's transcription, listed by George Lasry on Schmeh's blog in 2017 among the messages with no known decipherment. The readings, consolidated from the 2017 comment thread (Norbert, Armin, Baertl, Lasry), are routine traffic: march reports towards Belgrade, a repeat-telegram order, the Kertsch radio station, rouble rates after the break with the Soviet government; no decipherment of the other ten messages is known. No interference from the enemy. At midday 2 enemy divisions on the march towards Belgrade. p. 105. Germania, base (Etappe) Constantinople. For Mediterranean Division, re tel. no. 62. Div. telegram no. 58 done. 32141. Q4 [...] of 4 November dealt with. Admiralty Staff (Admiralstab). 32398. B. p. 109. O.K.M. evening report. S4V4. Quartering of the last elements completed. 1 further DU. Div 5 on the march towards Belgrade KAVV. 2. Otherwise no events. ASO. K511. p. 132. For EILVESE. Repeat telegram from fourth period in fifth. Prayer order 5 min. VVV. p. 146. Radio station Kertsch [Kerch] is operating. 1F. Call signs Richard Emil Karl. Notify the radio stations of that area. Chief of signals 4B. 7834. p. 171. In the Ukraine and Poland rouble rates rising sharply as a result of the break between Germany and the Soviet government and the expectation of the restoration of Russia by Germany and the Entente. p. 176. Breakthrough prepared. Whether the direction of the breakthrough will be to the north or north-east cannot yet be judged. p. 187 (part 1). Intercept Russian and Polish army traffic in full. Send anything important, especially from Polish traffic, enciphered by radio via the OHL [Supreme Army Command] station. p. 187 (part 2, AFAFF). As far as the teleprinter connection is not working. The rest in writing. To the chief. the same file: three messages read only in part (p. 164 F-G-X, p. 164 VFGAG, VGADA p. 215) and nine with no reading (pp. 73, 152, 153 VFVAX and AXVAA, 158, 170, 176 GGDAA, 189, 198); p. 217 is now its own entry decoded, not read Twelve of the 22 residue messages: three give fragments (Temesvar, Mirco; the Entente fleet at Kertsch with New Zealand, English and French divisions, VGADA, partial reading in texts/vgada_partial_reading.md); nine have no reading, because no known key fits them and several carry marked transmission gaps. A mechanical decode with holes in most sentences: shown so that the transcription and the key can be checked and improved, not as a reading. Click I can do this on a request. It opens a short form on GitHub with the request filled in: say how you will do it (visit, order, library) and roughly when, by month. The request is then marked as taken on this page, so two people do not go for the same leaf. When you have the images or the text, send them on the same issue, or by email if you do not use GitHub. Say whether the images may be shown on the site; they are always credited to you and to the archive. Before photographing, check the archive’s rules: most reading rooms allow it without flash, some ask for a form or a fee. A phone photograph of the whole page, flat, with the folio number visible, is enough for most requests; for a line in the gutter, one more of the page edge. Do not cut or mark anything to see better: say what you could not see and that closes the request too. Something not listed? Use the same form to propose a request. Each one here comes either from a write-up’s notes (its “Remaining gaps”, where the gap is marked as needing the archive) or from the catalogue , for every open item tagged “needs archive scans”; the list is rebuilt with the site. The ledger is archive_requests.json . Credit works as for every contribution: contribute .

DECODE R9407 is described as “Augurellio to …”, five pages, Partially decrypted , alphabet with graphic signs and numerals, language unknown; its date, 1475/1625, is the span of the whole volume, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591, the Bavarian ducal chancery’s collection of cipher keys with ciphertexts bound in among them. The record carries seven images. In the order of the text: P3, f. 233r : a full page of cipher, thirty-four lines, with a contemporary interlinear gloss over the first three lines and two clear Latin phrases inside the text. P5 : the second page, thirty-one lines, with a clear Latin sentence. P6, f. 235r : the third page, thirty-six lines, with one clear Latin phrase. The first pass took this image to be absent from the record; it is there, and it is the same leaf that image P4 shows at an angle beside the slip. P4, f. 234 : the slip ( Zettel ), eight lines written across the leaf, with the news from Belgrade, Datum ut in literis and the ciphered signature. P7 , the address leaf: two cipher lines of postscript, the signature again, and the superscription le[tte]re ad Mag[nifi]co domino Augurello that gave DECODE its title. P1–P2 , the outer address, in clear: Doctor Christof [W…], Bayrisch rhat, meinem freundlichen lieben bruder , with the docket 10. Decembris 33 and München . The images are not in the public domain, so no crop of them is reproduced here.

“Augurellio” is a name on the packet. The writer names himself inside, in cipher, at the foot of the slip and again at the foot of the address leaf, with the same fifteen signs both times: ʏ m ↓ I π ω ʏ □ 7 ϝ ʏ ʏx ÿ σ γ = I o r g W e i n m a i s t e r A faint later gloss over the second reads “… weinmeister”. The outer address sends the packet to the writer’s brother, a doctor and Bavarian councillor, for the dukes. The volume has a key made out for Augurelio (R9369, f. 172, Dno Aurelio Augurelio ), and that key is not this letter’s: in it ω stands for l, here for e. The date. The first pass dated the letter from its docket, read X Decembris 35 . The figures are small and cursive, and on the second pass they were taken as 33 ; the contents settle it. The letter reports King John’s army besieging László Móré in Palota with Hungarians, Turks and Bohemians, and says the besiegers are still before the castle. That is the siege Hieronymus Łaski opened on 14 April 1533 with Hassan Bey’s Turks and fifty Bohemian miners, and which ended when the walls were mined at the end of May, Ferdinand standing aside by agreement with his rival. The letter also mentions a castle taken the day after Easter (13 April 1533) and Ferdinand’s new peace with the Turk. It was written between late April and May 1533; the docket is a filing date, and the slip’s Datum ut in literis refers to the covering letters.

System A′ is a homophonic cipher of invented signs, Greek-looking letters and numerals, written without word division. Letters have one to three signs each (homophones), and several signs carry two values in this hand (polyphony): letters: ω e, □ n, 4 e, ч i, ʏx s, ÿ t, 3 u, x̸ u, ↓ r, γ r, 8 n, 5 a, φ a, δ l, ӏ h, I g, 7 m, 9 o, Δ f, 6 d, ⊔ c, ⊹ k, ⊕ t, Ψ ll, ⍴ rr; two-valued: ∃ d/ch, π w/b/o, o b/w, ‡‡ g/u, ʒ s/ch; ligatures: ʒo = h, ꝏ° = sp (so Caspar is c–a–[sp]–a–r); word signs: the hourglass ⧖ = “F.G.” , fürstliche Gnaden , the same sign as in the sibling key R9427, and distinct from the slashed x̸ that is u; the dotted ·ʃ· = King Ferdinand , fixed by seins herren [ʃ] … das er [ʃ] mit dem turcken ein frid gemacht ; and ∇ , the name of the man besieging Palota with herr Caspar, probably Łaski. clear figures: two numerals stand in the cipher as numerals, mit 4000 zu fuess und ross and hundert tausent und 34 tausent gulden .

The contemporary gloss over the first lines of f. 233 reads Genedig fursten und herren … Caspar … das leger , and that is how the letter opens. The full decipherment, line by line, with open words marked, is in the repository ( targets/augurelio1535/pass2/reading.txt ). Below, the German of the main passages and what they say. f. 233r: the siege of Palota Genedig fursten und herren, … ich zu herrn Caspar in das leger fur den Palota hab geschickt … Rerum novarum autem quod hic habemus … sol ich euer F.G. wie hernach volgt verstendigen, das er durch den [∇] und herr Casparn mit 4000 zu fuess und ross, ungern, turcken und Behamen, mechtigen ungern, … het in ainem festen schloss Palota genent belegern lassen, der lange zeit grosse merderei hat getriben, und von baidern auf dem tag zu Bresburg ist ausgeschlossen, also das ieder kunig, welcher zuvor kombt, straffen mag … umb hundert tausent und 34 tausent gulden geschetzt hat; und wiewol erstlich gedachts schloss nit nach herr Casparn rat vergeblich beschossen ist worden, iedoch hofft er es mit graben und maurwerch auszerichten. Herr Caspar has been sent into the camp before Palota. King John has had the strong castle of Palota besieged by [∇] and herr Caspar with four thousand foot and horse, Hungarians, Turks and Bohemians: its holder has long carried on great murder and robbery, and at the diet of Pressburg both kings left him out of the settlement, so that whichever king comes first may punish him. The castle was valued at 134,000 gulden. It was first bombarded to no effect, against herr Caspar’s advice; now he hopes to take it by digging and undermining. The Latin Et propter illum hominem plures introduces those who have tried to get the castle relieved: this has not been permitted by [ʃ], Ferdinand, who thinks he has a peace with the Turk. So a Hungarian, Török Bálint , who one evening went drinking with [ʃ] at Vienna, was dispatched about the relief with the answer that he should come back and speak of such things in the morning, wan er nuechter sei , when he is sober. The Hungarians of his party took it as a great insult, and so the bishop of Veszprém was sent to [ʃ] with the message that everything done at Pressburg, at Constantinople and elsewhere had been done without their knowledge; they could not tell whether they had been given away or sold. P5: the truce, Katzianer, Simontornya, the post Their lord has always fed them with many words, which misled them more than it helped; now he must tell them where they stand. Before he left, [one of them] wrote to Katzianer ( Cacianer ) to ask what to expect of the truce and whether it would be extended. Katzianer answered that he had consulted his lord’s council and was to tell him, on behalf of his lord [ʃ], that [ʃ] mit dem turcken ein frid gemacht and would keep to it; he and his lord should keep the peace too and von der belegerung des More Lesl[o] abziechen , raise the siege of László Móré, or something would be undertaken against them and the castle relieved. Regardless of this threatening letter, [∇] and herr Caspar marched on the castle with many men and are still before it; they also took another castle, with much booty, the day after Easter, man heist s Simontornia, ist ser fest : Simontornya . Illud tamen summum maximum esse existimo, das euer F.G. Hansen Schetinger, burger und kaufman zu Munchen, handlen und genedigklich zusprechen, das er zu Wien seinem factor, wan er doselbs grossen handel fuert, bevelch gebe, das er alle brief, so ime von herr Caspar oder von der […] zukomen, on allen verzug euer F.G. alweg zuschicke … The main request: the dukes should have Hans Schetinger, burgher and merchant of Munich, tell his factor at Vienna, where he does a large trade, to forward at once every letter from herr Caspar; he could do it secretly. If the dukes dealt with Schetinger in this way, they would not need to use den iuden any further, dan im nit zu vertrauen ist . f. 235r: the Jew, Minckwitz, herr Caspar, the Chancellor The reason: the Jew let the letters be copied at Kraków before he delivered them, as he admitted to the writer himself, and as the dukes will learn from him. A secretary told the writer that he had seen at Kraków copies of the dukes’ letters in the hands of Minckwitz , and that they are common knowledge there. Minckwitz, the Saxon feuder, is at feud with [∇] and they have written each other letters of defiance; he has no other refuge, and no one knows what he might do with such copies: wil das als euern F.G. [un]gehorsamer undertenigkait aus schuldiger pflicht haben angezaigt, damit kain ander der hendlung wissend vertacht werde. After the Latin Quid autem actum sit : the writer has dealt with [a man whose name is not deciphered], told him of the dukes’ good will and offer, and he thanked them warmly and is glad to serve them; he has been told to treat with the Turk on their behalf, so that if [ʃ] makes peace with the Turk, [ʃ] should have peace with all his allies too, though without naming anyone, which he is willing to do. Herr Caspar bit in aller gehorsamer undertenigkait, euer F.G. wellen ine und seine kind genedigklich bedencken : herr Caspar asks the dukes to remember him and his children. All letters should go through Schetinger. The writer encloses a copy of a letter that [ʃ]’s councillor, now in Turkey, wrote to the regents at Vienna. As far as he understands, the Chancellor is also going to Constantinople, and he will report what is negotiated there, and keep a careful watch on the news. The slip on f. 234, and the postscript [Wiss]en: heut dato ist ein Ratz komen mit briefen, der sagt, wie zu Kriechischen Weissenburg funfczig tausent turcken sind ausgezogen hieher auf Ofen zu … doch nit was fur ein frid ist, wie dan euer F.G. aus [dem] schreiben zu vernemen haben, ist zu besorgen; auch wie mir er selbs het gesagt, der [ʃ] werde mer krieg dan frid haben. Datum ut in literis. Jirg Weinmaister. Today a Rascian (a Serb) came with letters and says that fifty thousand Turks have marched out of Belgrade towards Buda ; what kind of peace this is, the dukes can judge from the letters; it is to be feared, as the man himself said, that Ferdinand will have more war than peace. The slip is dated “as in the letters”, which is also what the faint later gloss over the line says. The postscript on the address leaf commends the writer to the dukes as his most gracious lords and is signed again.

The key of R9369, the one addressed to Augurelio, was tried first and rejected against the gloss. The letter’s system was recognised from the gloss pairs as System A′, and the key recovered from the R9427 gloss and extended on R9410 was carried across by the shapes of the signs, which gave running German at once. First pass. Candidate values for each sign were estimated statistically against a letter-trigram model of German, the most probable text was decoded and then rescored with word frequencies from the Deutsches Textarchiv; rounds of manual correction followed, each aligned back to the signs to re-estimate the key; about forty transcription corrections on the two main pages. Result: f. 233 and the P5 page at about 96%, the angled column 65%. Second pass. The record’s image list was taken from DECODE and P6 fetched. All pages were transcribed again, one character per sign; a solver (simulated annealing) against a language model of sixteenth-century German, started from the System A′ key with the gloss values fixed, gave German on every page. A decoder that chooses the value of each two-valued sign by context then decoded each line, and every line was compared with its crop. That separated the hourglass F.G. from the slashed u, found the clear numerals, the ligature mγ , the name signs, and several dozen single misreadings. History. Hungarian accounts of the 1533 siege of Palota (Łaski, Hassan Bey, the Czech miners, Móré) confirmed the decipherment of More Lesl[o] and Behamen and fixed the date. The measure is a word count over the decipherment: a word counts only when its sense is not in doubt. 1,003 words, 33 open (30 words and three occurrences of ∇): 96.7% . The key carried back to the siblings. On 2 October 2026 the key as improved on this letter was carried back by sign shape to the five sibling letters of System A′ (R9408, R9409, R9410, R9413, R9427), re-learned on each letter and checked by a hand decipherment of every line. The share of each machine decipherment that segments into period German words rose from 0.55–0.69 with the older gloss key to 0.84–0.88, and the hand decipherments give sense for 83.9% of the words of the six letters. R9408 turned out to be a second letter of Jörg Weinmeister, from Buda (Ofen) on 8 February 1534, and R9410 holds a Latin letter of King John Zápolya to the dukes of 30 June 1534. The letters are on the KAA 4591 page.

About thirty scattered words , at most two or three on a line, whose signs are legible but give no word under the values the letter uses: among them the opening words of f. 233r line 1, a word before “turcken” (l. 5), the man before “zum [ʃ] geschickt” (l. 31), and a few words at the end of P5 (ll. 27–28). Every one was retried with the extended key and at the image. ∇ , the name sign of the man who besieges Palota with herr Caspar (four occurrences): probably Hieronymus Łaski, who led the siege (grade C). Herr Caspar himself is not identified. One name at the head of f. 235r l. 16, the man the writer dealt with on the dukes’ behalf. Grades: the passages quoted above are C (key and context agree), except Ratz on the slip and Hansen Schetinger (spelt Schotinger later), which are M ; the surname of the doctor on the outer address is not made out.

Two cipher dispatches of the Charleston commandant to Cornwallis (March 1781) and his letter to Stewart (August 1781), taken by the Americans and filed in the Papers of the Continental Congress with a decipherment between the lines. The ring key of the British “Common cipher” and its moving setting were rebuilt from it, and all 6,349 numbers deciphered again by program: 99.8% English, control 0–2%. Saberton had found no evidence these ciphers were broken. 33 · 19 · 37 · 45 · 31 — 24 · 50 · 8 · 69 · 16 — 3 · 11 · 14 · 73 · 18 · 17 · 14 · 3 · 19 · 26 [A = 19] · t · – · h · – · e · p · r · i · – · n · c · i · p · a · l ring 5 24 29 1 25 23 22 6 19 9 17 13 16 7 12 8 14 15 26 4 18 21 3 2 11 · 30 and over = fillers Charleston → Lord Cornwallis · ring cipher with moving setting · March and August 1781 · read from the contemporary decipherment Nisbet Balfour’s intercepted cipher dispatches, 1781 (Papers of the Continental Congress, item 51) to Lord Cornwallis Go to the full text ↓ The British commandant at Charleston reported to Cornwallis in a number cipher that the Americans took and deciphered; the key was rebuilt from their decipherment and every letter deciphered again from the numbers. Nisbet Balfour, commandant at Charleston, to Lord Cornwallis in North Carolina: one dispatch on three numbered sheets and a second letter, both of early March 1781. A third letter, to Lt Col. Alexander Stewart, 12 August 1781, is in clear with cipher runs. Where National Archives, Washington, RG 360, Papers of the Continental Congress, item 51 (Intercepted Letters) vol. 1, pp. 717–736 (catalog naId 475670722, images 562–579). The cipher The southern British “Common cipher”: 25 numbers in a fixed ring turned against the alphabet. A group of fillers with one real number sets which number stands for A, and the setting changes 35 times. The Stewart letter uses a different, fixed table. How it was deciphered Every cipher page carries a decipherment between the lines, probably James Lovell’s. The ring order and the setting rule were rebuilt from it; the 6,349 transcribed numbers were then deciphered by program alone, and checked against the interlinear and a control. What it says Charleston news for Cornwallis: Marion’s and Lee’s raid on Monk’s Corner, Craig’s seizure of Wilmington, Sumter beaten off at the Congarees, Arnold’s plan for the Albemarle Sound, Rodney’s capture of St Eustatius. Still open Four numbers of the Stewart table (five tokens) and twelve illegible numbers at page edges. The Cornwallis, Wemyss and Craig cipher passages in the same volume, whose translations are on pp. 759–761, were not transcribed.

Volume 1 of the Intercepted Letters in the Papers of the Continental Congress holds British letters taken by the Americans between 1775 and 1781. The National Archives catalogue describes them as including “letters in cipher (some decoded) exchanged between General Charles Cornwallis and Colonel Nisbet Balfour, 1780–1781”. The image descriptions supplied by Fold3 (one per digitised page) were filtered for cipher, Cornwallis and Balfour, which found these items: A. Balfour to Cornwallis, Nos. 1–3, pp. 717–725 (images 562–570), wholly in cipher, with a letter-by-letter decipherment written over every line. The docket on p. 728 reads “Letters dated the … March 1781 … in Cypher … supposed Balfour to Cornwallis”. The three sheets are one dispatch: the last words of No. 1 run on into the first word of No. 2 (“their post near Heron’s / bridge”). B. Balfour to Cornwallis, pp. 729–732 (images 572–575), wholly in cipher, interlinear decipherment, docketed “Balfour to Cornwallis, about March 1781”. C. Balfour at Charleston to Lt Col. Alexander Stewart, 12 August 1781, pp. 733–736 (images 576–579): clear text with runs of cipher, most of them with the decipherment over them; signed N. Balfour. The dates come from the text. No. 1 reports the Chatham’s arrival on 29 January, the raid on Monk’s Corner on 2 February and Craig’s letter of 28 February; No. 2 reports Sumter’s attack on the Congarees on the “nineteenth ult.” (19 February), so the dispatch is of March. B has Rodney’s capture of St Eustatius (3 February) and news of Arnold at Portsmouth on 10 February. The opening of No. 1. The first group, 33 19 37 45 31, sets the cipher: 19 stands for A. Over the numbers the decipherer wrote “the principal occurrences since you left us are the arrival of the Chatham…”. Image: National Archives, RG 360, Papers of the Continental Congress, item 51 vol. 1, p. 717 (image 562, Fold3 file 407629), via the National Archives Catalog.

Ian Saberton described this cipher in 2019 from letters in the Cornwallis Papers: an inner ring of numbers turned against an alphabet, the number standing for A given first, and numbers of 30 and over as fillers. The letters here fit that description exactly, and the transcription gives the whole ring: The ring. 25 numbers in a fixed cyclic order, 5 24 29 1 25 23 22 6 19 9 17 13 16 7 12 8 14 15 26 4 18 21 3 2 11 (1–29 without 10, 20, 27 and 28), against a 25-letter alphabet with i and j as one letter. With A set to 19 the table is a19 b9 c17 d13 e16 f7 g12 h8 i14 k15 l26 m4 n18 o21 p3 q2 r11 s5 t24 u29 v1 w25 x23 y22 z6. Fillers. Numbers of 30 and over mean nothing and are scattered through the words (24 50 8 69 16 = “the”). The setting moves. A group of fillers holding one real number resets A to that number. The decipherer marked each such group with a brace. No. 1 has 13 of them, No. 2 has 15, No. 3 has 3 and B has 4. Nos. 2 and 3 start without one and carry on with the previous sheet’s last setting. Numerals in clear. A number standing alone between dashes is a numeral: the 82nd, 84th, 71st and 64th regiments, dates (29 January, 28 February, 26), a French 64-gun ship, 18 men and 40 horses. On p. 718 the encipherer slipped: the indicator group 47 49 31 25 40 would set A to 25, but the decipherer underlined the 25 and wrote “should be 13”. With 13 the text goes on “two troops under Colonel Fenwick”; with 25 it does not read. This decipherer was working from the numbers, not copying a clear text. p. 718: the indicator 47 49 31 25 40 under its brace, with “should be 13” written beneath the 25. Image: National Archives, RG 360, Papers of the Continental Congress, item 51 vol. 1, p. 718 (image 563, Fold3 file 407632), via the National Archives Catalog. The Stewart letter of August is in another cipher: one fixed table with no settings, the numbers 12–38 for letters and 40 and over as fillers. Over a run the decipherer wrote “day notice is sent”, and the fifteen numbers under it, fillers removed, match the fifteen letters one for one (d32 a31 y29 n35 o16 t37 i24 c22 e13 s27). Its table, rebuilt from the interlinear, is a31 b12 c22 d32 e13 f23 g33 h14 i24 k34 l15 m25 n35 o16 p26 r17 s27 t37 u18 v28 w38 y29, with e also 1.

Word division, capitals and punctuation are editorial. Numbers that stand in clear in the cipher are printed as numerals. The cipher’s spellings are kept (“governer”, “offisers”, “cary sfort”). No. 1. The principal occurrences since you left us are the arrival of the Chatham with convoy from Europe, Governor Bull and Sir Egerton Leigh passengers, both of which are now at the Board of Police. Fifty thousand pounds came in the Chatham; she arrived 29 January. A party of Marion and Lee surprised the sergeant’s party at Monk’s Corner on the 2 February, killed two and made some prisoners, which, with burning three waggons and carrying off some horses, was all they effected. Colonel Small with the 84 and fifty Hessians marched immediately there; the church was fortified and the inhabitants’ horses ordered in to mount the infantry there, as well as at Neilson’s, where fifty men are placed. Two troops under Colonel Fenwick and Lieutenant Campbell, 71 regiment, raising and in forwardness. The light company of the 84 sent to Pocotaligo to cover that country from plunderers. The 82 with convalescents of the army took possession of Wilmington the 28 January without opposition; the enemy were driven from their post at Heron’s Bridge by Major Craig; the marines and seamen landed and a post close to the town taken, which is now in a state of defence not to be forced but by a large corps [with] cannon. Craig is informed of your movements so far as we know them. Tho’ not afraid of the militia now against him, wishes much for a reinforcement; this is not in my power to send. He has all the articles wanted by the army and is perfectly safe. His last letter, 28 February, mentions the enemy being about six hundred and in their post near Heron’s No. 2. Bridge. If you mean to communicate by Cross Creek the banks of the river must be cleared, as the enemy have posts on it. Georgetown was attacked and Colonel Campbell with some few men taken prisoners as they slept in a house out of the redoubt. Some small parties of men have since been at that post, from the bad conduct of the officers. Fanning’s is now moved from thence and joined Watson’s corps; a detachment of one hundred men are now in Georgetown under Captain Gray of Fanning’s. A fleet from Ireland with provisions and stores under convoy of the Assurance arrived 23 ult., and being in want of water put into this and Beaufort before they proceed to York. A packet from England with duplicates of the dispatches by Ross 20 ult. On the last of February a packet sailed for England with accounts of your being at Salem and the state of affairs here. An express from General Arnold in the Chesapeak 23 ultimo, informing of a French 64 and two frigates having blocked up that place, and desiring assistance. This letter was shewn to Captain Barclay, who altho’ possessed of the Chatham, Carysfort, Assurance, Galatea and Blonde, would not proceed in quest of the enemy. The Chatham with her convoy sailed 26 for New York. Sumpter, having raised at least three hundred men, attacked Congarees nineteenth ult., but by the conduct of Maxwell was beat off; at Thompson’s he had the same fate and was forced to cross the Santee. Lord Rawdon moved with great speed after him to Congarees, Camden and Sumpter’s [?], detaching 64 and York Volunteers in such directions as gave reason to expect the success his movements merited, by misconduct in No. 3. some of the detachments and other unforeseen events he only got at him as he crossed the river, by Watson’s corps, which acted with […] and drove him with the loss of 18 men and 40 horses; we lost none. Watson is now in pursuit of him, and Marion with the [Hightown?] and Fanning’s. Lord Rawdon is also towards [Pedee?] No. 3 ends at the foot of its sheet; no further sheet survives in the volume.

The same ring and the same setting rule decipher it unchanged, with four indicators (A = 23, 18, 6, 5). In Gen. Arnold’s letter is the following paragraph: “If the cooperation will be of service, I intend to send some boats with four or five hundred men through Currituck Inlet to sweep the Albemarle Sound as high as Edenton, and to go to Newbern and destroy their shipping, stores &c., while a few armed vessels take post at Ocracock Bar and a frigate cruises without.” The General’s intentions to prosecute this plan is corroborated by Capt. Eyons of the Charlestown, who arrived yesterday from Gardner’s Bay; left Arnold at Portsmouth on the tenth of Feb[ruary]. By the progress of Arnold, his operations are mentioned in a newspaper. By the bearer [?]: the removal of the French and intelligence of your movements are both necessary before Arnold proceeds to execute his plan. I have sent him by Evans the cypher, in case he can communicate with you. Evans left this today, being sent to collect the force here, which is now dispersed, to attack the French in the Chesapeak, and proceeds to try to get to Arnold. Having reason to believe the enemy are gone from thence [Savannah?] is well, but seriously alarmed for want of provisions; the river Savannah must shortly be our dependance for supplying that post. The enemy make such serious inroads [and] raise such force that I fear, without an addition soon to our corps on the frontier, we shall be awkwardly situated. A fortunate stroke at Sumpter and Marian will do much. What is to be done with the troops from England, if they come, as is expected, here? What is to become of the post at Wilmington if your movements leave that place uncovered by your army? The bearer, I believe, if he delivers this, he must be well rewarded; he is to proceed to Philadelphia and will be useful there if you wish it. Scott’s letter is a blind. Sir George Rodney has taken possession of St Eustatia, has engaged a Dutch line of battle ship, taken her and a large fleet of merchantmen under convoy for Holland, so that I think there is no kind of doubt a war with the Dutch must take place. “I have sent him by Evans the cypher”: Balfour sent Arnold a copy of this cipher, which Saberton identifies as the one Arnold and later Leslie used with Cornwallis in Virginia.

A clear letter, “Charles Town August 12th 1781”, to the commander of the field army after Rawdon’s departure, with the sensitive parts in cipher. The cipher runs, in order (the clear text between them is in the transcription): … the escort will not be at Martin’s till Tuesday [?] … day notice is sent … detachment to wait [?] … for the militia will not keep Orangeburgh … possible at present to supply a post there; our present communication assisted by water carriage … keep it … two hundred guineas are rent [?] … spare, or is safe to send at once … not one dragoon is here; employed to the southward getting provisions, rice … your mounted convalescents belonging to your army … by then [the next?] escort … officers when recovered … as to Thomson, I am clear he will be better here; very dangerous; be assured [it] is greatly to be guarded against, as we are vulnerable in so many posts. The depot near Monk’s Corner put in a state of defence … to get possession of the boats upon the Santee by means of the negroes … the garrison [?] … Caldwell near you, but is not to act with the cavalry, by Lord Rawdon’s directions … from your intelligence that the enemy are in force on the other side low down, cross either at Manigault’s or Murray’s ferries, intercept the escort; a small movement of a corps towards Nelson’s would effectually cover them, if convenient. The two volumes of Intercepted Letters (848 images) were listed through the National Archives Catalog’s records API. The pages were fetched as JPEG 2000 and cut into strips, and three transcription agents copied every number, the interlinear letters and the decipherer’s marks: 6,349 cipher tokens on 17 pages. A single number-to-letter table per sheet, aligned against the interlinear, agreed only 20–27%: the table changes inside a sheet. Saberton’s ring, given a setting for each word, read in long runs. A 25-letter alphabet fixed the remaining i/j and h/i slips, and then one ring order fitted every page. The braced groups proved to be the setting indicators. From then on the decoder ( decode.py ) works from the numbers alone: it reads an indicator’s number as A, skips fillers and prints lone numbers as numerals. Where an indicator has only two fillers and could also be the word “a” padded with fillers, the next 40 letters are scored both ways with the project’s English model. The only outside correction is the decipherer’s “should be 13”. Two fillers cut off at the page edge on p. 722 were restored as “4x” from the visible first digit, which completed two indicators. Measured on the decoder’s output, a letter counts as read when a 24-letter window containing it scores at least −3.3 per letter on the en-modern model. No. 1: 1,213 of 1,213; No. 2: 1,292 of 1,292; No. 3: 237 of 237; B: 1,530 of 1,539; Stewart: 850 of 850. The same measure on the same numbers deciphered with a corrupted ring gives 0–2%. The project’s validation test ( docs/_validate.py ) scores the reading at −2.24 per letter, against −7.26 for random keys of the same shape and −4.16 for a key refitted to shuffled ciphertext: pass. Against the interlinear as transcribed, the decoder agrees on 62–82% of letters where the interlinear is legible. The differences checked are faint or misread interlinear letters. The one real disagreement is in No. 3, where the cipher has the numeral 18 for the men lost and the decipherer wrote “fifteen”.

Grade C for the words around them. Twelve numbers in A and B illegible on the microfilm scan (page edges of pp. 718 and 724, blots); each falls inside a word that otherwise reads. No. 2, after “Sumpter’s”, and No. 3, after “acted with”: a word the cipher does not give (grade I). “Hightown” and “Pedee” at the end of No. 3 are conjectures for “hitown” and “s?edee” (grade C). Stewart letter: “Tuesday”, “rent” and “the next” are grade C; the runs are short, and the clear text between them has not been edited here. The cipher passages of Cornwallis to Wemyss and to Balfour (7 October 1780) and Craig to Cornwallis (23 July 1781), in the same volume, were not transcribed; their numbered translations are on pp. 759–761. The decipherer’s hand is not signed. James Lovell broke the cipher of Clinton and Cornwallis in 1781, and these pages are probably his work, but the hand has not been compared with his.

Balfour to Cornwallis, Charleston, early March 1781, Nos. 1-3 (pp. 717-725) **No. 1.** The principal occurrences since you left us are the arrival of the Chatham with convoy from Europe, Governor Bull and Sir Egerton Leigh passengers, both of which are now at the Board of Police. Fifty thousand pounds came in the Chatham; she arrived 29 January. A party of Marion and Lee surprised the sergeant's party at Monk's Corner on the 2 February, killed two and made some prisoners, which, with burning three waggons and carrying off some horses, was all they effected. Colonel Small with the 84 and fifty Hessians marched immediately there; the church was fortified and the inhabitants' horses ordered in to mount the infantry there, as well as at Neilson's, where fifty men are placed. Two troops under Colonel Fenwick and Lieutenant Campbell, 71 regiment, raising and in forwardness. The light company of the 84 sent to Pocotaligo to cover that country from plunderers. The 82 with convalescents of the army took possession of Wilmington the 28 January without opposition; the enemy were driven from their post at Heron's Bridge by Major Craig; the marines and seamen landed and a post close to the town taken, which is now in a state of defence not to be forced but by a large corps [with] cannon. Craig is informed of your movements so far as we know them. Tho' not afraid of the militia now against him, wishes much for a reinforcement; this is not in my power to send. He has all the articles wanted by the army and is perfectly safe. His last letter, 28 February, mentions the enemy being about six hundred and in their post near Heron's **No. 2.** Bridge. If you mean to communicate by Cross Creek the banks of the river must be cleared, as the enemy have posts on it. Georgetown was attacked and Colonel Campbell with some few men taken prisoners as they slept in a house out of the redoubt. Some small parties of men have since been at that post, from the bad conduct of the officers. Fanning's is now moved from thence and joined Watson's corps; a detachment of one hundred men are now in Georgetown under Captain Gray of Fanning's. A fleet from Ireland with provisions and stores under convoy of the Assurance arrived 23 ult., and being in want of water put into this and Beaufort before they proceed to York. A packet from England with duplicates of the dispatches by Ross 20 ult. On the last of February a packet sailed for England with accounts of your being at Salem and the state of affairs here. An express from General Arnold in the Chesapeak 23 ultimo, informing of a French 64 and two frigates having blocked up that place, and desiring assistance. This letter was shewn to Captain Barclay, who altho' possessed of the Chatham, Carysfort, Assurance, Galatea and Blonde, would not proceed in quest of the enemy. The Chatham with her convoy sailed 26 for New York. Sumpter, having raised at least three hundred men, attacked Congarees nineteenth ult., but by the conduct of Maxwell was beat off; at Thompson's he had the same fate and was forced to cross the Santee. Lord Rawdon moved with great speed after him to Congarees, Camden and Sumpter's [?], detaching 64 and York Volunteers in such directions as gave reason to expect the success his movements merited, by misconduct in **No. 3.** some of the detachments and other unforeseen events he only got at him as he crossed the river, by Watson's corps, which acted with [...] and drove him with the loss of 18 men and 40 horses; we lost none. Watson is now in pursuit of him, and Marion with the [Hightown?] and Fanning's. Lord Rawdon is also towards [Pedee?] Notes. "[Hightown?]" is "hitown"; "[Pedee?]" is "s?edee" at the foot of the sheet, where the letter breaks off. B. Balfour to Cornwallis, Charleston, about March 1781 (pp. 729-732) In Gen. Arnold's letter is the following paragraph: "If the cooperation will be of service, I intend to send some boats with four or five hundred men through Currituck Inlet to sweep the Albemarle Sound as high as Edenton, and to go to Newbern and destroy their shipping, stores &c., while a few armed vessels take post at Ocracock Bar and a frigate cruises without." The General's intentions to prosecute this plan is corroborated by Capt. Eyons of the Charlestown, who arrived yesterday from Gardner's Bay; left Arnold at Portsmouth on the tenth of Feb[ruary]. By the progress of Arnold, his operations are mentioned in a newspaper. By the bearer [?]: the removal of the French and intelligence of your movements are both necessary before Arnold proceeds to execute his plan. I have sent him by Evans the cypher, in case he can communicate with you. Evans left this today, being sent to collect the force here, which is now dispersed, to attack the French in the Chesapeak, and proceeds to try to get to Arnold. Having reason to believe the enemy are gone from thence [Savannah?] is well, but seriously alarmed for want of provisions; the river Savannah must shortly be our dependance for supplying that post. The enemy make such serious inroads [and] raise such force that I fear, without an addition soon to our corps on the frontier, we shall be awkwardly situated. A fortunate stroke at Sumpter and Marian will do much. What is to be done with the troops from England, if they come, as is expected, here? What is to become of the post at Wilmington if your movements leave that place uncovered by your army? The bearer, I believe, if he delivers this, he must be well rewarded; he is to proceed to Philadelphia and will be useful there if you wish it. Scott's letter is a blind. Sir George Rodney has taken possession of St Eustatia, has engaged a Dutch line of battle ship, taken her and a large fleet of merchantmen under convoy for Holland, so that I think there is no kind of doubt a war with the Dutch must take place. Notes. "By the bearer" is the end of a sentence in the cipher ("...in a newspaper by the bearer"); its place is uncertain. The "&" before "Marian" and in "French & proceeds" is a cross sign, not a number (the decipherer wrote "&" over it on p. 731). C. Balfour to Lt Col. Alexander Stewart, 12 Aug 1781 (pp. 733-736), cipher runs Arrangements for an escort and supplies to Stewart's army: no dragoons at Charleston, the depot near Monk's Corner put in defence, Caldwell not to act with the cavalry, and a request to cover the escort at Manigault's or Murray's ferries with a move towards Nelson's. A four-page Latin cipher letter on the Sforza marriage alliance with the new king of Hungary, with the dowry raised from 150,000 to 200,000 ducats. Harrison Bornstein recovered the key from the clear minute kept in Milan and read 561 of 624 words (89.9%), under the 95% bar. In christo pater et domine pater honorande … (four pages of homophonic cipher, about 60 signs for the letters of Latin) Milan → Buda · homophonic Latin cipher · 30 November 1490 · key from external plaintext Maffeo da Treviglio to Tamás Bakócz, 1490 Go to the full text ↓ A Milanese envoy tells the chancellor of Hungary that the Duke will raise the dowry for a Sforza bride from 150,000 to 200,000 ducats; 90% deciphered with a key recovered through the clear minute kept in Milan. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 4 November 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on plaintext from external sources · Extent: partial (90% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Harrison Bornstein (solution) · Also credited · Vestigia (Hungarian documents in the Archivio di Stato di Milano) (key or decipherment used) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) external text At a glance Key from external plaintext · partial (90% of the cipher) The letter Maffeo da Treviglio, the Milanese agent who had negotiated the Sforza–Corvinus match since 1489, writes from Milan on 30 November 1490 to Tamás Bakócz, bishop of Győr and chancellor of the King of Hungary. The salutation, closing, date, signature and address are in clear. Where Hungarian National Archives (MNL OL), Diplomatikai Levéltár, DL 46150 (Hungaricana charter 228061). Four paper pages in cipher. Catalogue item 1235. The cipher A homophonic Latin cipher of letter-like signs, figures and marks: 76 labels over 3,199 tokens, about 60 of them carrying the text. It is not Maffeo’s 1489 key. How it was deciphered The key was recovered from the clear minute of the same letter kept in Milan, then extended in a retry pass. Doubtful transcriptions were checked on the image. The statistical validation passed. What it says After King Matthias’s death the planned marriage of Bianca Maria Sforza to John Corvinus had lapsed, and the new king, Vladislas II, took up the “affinity” himself. Maffeo reports the Duke’s warm welcome of the offer and says that, having come down to 150,000 ducats, he now offers 200,000, in jewels or money at the King’s choice, with 10,000 for the bride’s trousseau. Bakócz is to send the courier back, with envoys or the King’s decision. Still open 63 words are not read as sense: 8 on ambiguous signs, 15 on letter signs standing once for a title or phrase, and others on lost or single-use signs. The images were not seen here. Credit Harrison Bornstein (PR #199) supplied the Hungaricana images and directed the transcription, broke it ciphertext-only to 79% of words, rebuilt the key from the Milan minute, and read it.
buda1490.html#the-letter

Maffeo reports his audience in Buda with the king, Bianca Maria’s part in the affair and the Chancellor of Bohemia, and the Duke’s reception of the offer. He presents the alliance as the continuation of the bond with King Matthias. On the dowry he says the King’s demand had seemed to exceed all measure and made the Duke hesitate, since no king had ever received such a sum. He asks Bakócz to send the courier back at once. The Latin and an English translation are under Full texts.
buda1490.html#the-key

The key has several homophones for the common letters: five signs for e , four for i , four for a and five for s . Some signs have two or three values by context (for example qA is s , i or t ). The letter minute in Milan gave the plain text against which the key was rebuilt. That makes the minute a partial check, not an independent one: the notes set out how far it can count as evidence. A second Maffeo key, “Cum Mafeo Triviliensi” (DECODE R5407), may be the key of this cipher; that was checked only as far as one session could.
buda1490.html#the-reading

561 of 624 words (89.9%) are read as sense, up from 544 (87.2%) before the retry pass. That is under the 95% bar, so this is a partial reading. The 39 transcription suspects were checked on the image: 11 fixed, 19 confirmed as the writer’s own departures, 9 left ambiguous.
buda1490.html#uncertain

8 words rest on signs the image check left ambiguous ( dominationem , cepit , semper , adduxit , secundum , reuerendissime , descendit , responso ); only the original would settle them. 15 words rest on letter signs that stand once for a title or phrase (such as Bianca and the Chancellor of Bohemia), known from the minute only. 4 words rest on signs with no value at that place, and 9 more are the writer’s own departures (grade I). 15 words have letters left out or multi-sign departures; the shape check on the page images is still to do. 12 words have a lost sign, mostly on page 3 lines 15–21, filled from the minute.

In christo pater et domine pater honorande. ## Page 1 Non [?citius] quam ad uigesimam diem [?presentis] mensis potui ad Illustrissimum Principem meum peruenire. Cui captata oportunitate fideliter exposui operam factam per Reuerendissimam [?Dominationem] Vestram circa afinitatem quam contrahi [?cepit] inter Serenissimum Dominum Regem Hungarie et prefatum Illustrissimum Dominum meum, medio [...] [...] [...] eius sororis, et quemadmodum ultimo ex parte ipsius uocatus fui Budam et ab ea introductus ad prefatu Serenissimum Dominum Regem, et demum id quod dictum et tractatum fuit mecum per ipsam simul cum [...] [...] [...] [...], quibus Serenissimus Dominus Rex rem ipsam tractandam commiserat. Excepit [?mea] [?ex] animo eius [?Excellentia] audiitque libentissime Serenissimum Dominum Regem bene dispositum esse ad contrahendam secum afinitatem. Cuius cum ex uerbis meis Reuerendissimam quoque Dominationem Vestram studiosissimam cognouerit, quamquam ad eam precipue inclinare debeat [?Serenissimi] [...] [...] [...] [...] Regni beneficio, ⟨tamen⟩ nihil dubitans quin feruentior etiam ad eam [?reddatur], eo [?amicissimo] afectu quem [?semper] erga ipsam habuisse [?ostendit] ab eo tempore quo cum Serenissimo quondam Rege Mathia felicis memorie de afinitate agi ceptum est usque in presentem diem: si antea ipsam Reuerendissimam Dominationem Vestram amabat non mediocriter, nunc inter precipuos et raros amicos recepit; et quanto eficacius ipsius erga eius Excellentiam afectus bonis operibus comprobatus est, tanto plus incrementi eius erga ## Page 2 ipsam amor suscepit, cuius procul dubio [?uberrimum] [?fructum] sentiet quandocumque tempus patietur. Affinitas Serenissimi Domini Regis [...] uestri mirum in modum Illustrissimo Principi meo grata est, quoniam, preterquam quod ab eius Excellentia sumo semper amore et beniuolentia Maiestatem suam prosecuta sit etiam antequam ad illud Regnum ascenderet, et [?propter] regiam dignitatem et [?propter] singularem eius animi bonitatem, cum eius intentio fuerit per affinitatem quam cum Rege Mathia cotraxerat cum Regno uestro coniungi, [...] quod ipse Dominus Rex a uobis euectus fuit, sibi persuadebit, quando hec affinitas procedat, in ea que prius cepta fuerat continuasse, non noua [?iniuisse]. Verum est quod suma dotis per Maiestatem suam [?petita], [?quemadmodum] uisa est modum excedere, ita Illustrissimum Principem meum in ⟨aliquam⟩ suspensionem [?adduxit]. Durum enim ei uisum est, ut ego quoque Reuerendissime Dominationi Vestre comemoraui, quod ea suma a se expeti debeat quam neque ullus unquam Rex quamlibet magnus dotis nomine accepit, neque [?uideat] a quibus haberi possit. Sed quando prefata Maiestas regia ad hanc affinitatem inclinet, quemadmodum et ipsa et uos [?alias] michi afirmastis, Excellentia Principis mei contenta erit cum aliqua additione dotis supra illud quod quondam [?Regi] Mathie [?promiserat] [?ostendere] se et dignitatis domus et nobilitatis sanguinis eius bonam habere ## Page 3 uelle rationem. Et sicut prius descenderat ad centum quinquaginta milia ducatorum, nunc et usque ad ducenta milia se extendet, siue in ea [...] partem iocalium recipere uelit siue pecuniam habere uelit tantum cupiat, quod arbitrio Maiestatis regie relinquetur, eo excepto quod si pecuniam tantum uoluerit, sciat ex dicta [...] [...] [...] decem milia in uestitu sponse necessarie exponenda [...]; de iocalibus uero prefata Regia Maiestas honorifice [?secundum] utriusque partis dignitatem prouidere teneatur. Et que suma ducentorum milium ut magna est, ita quisque dignissimus et eminentissimus Rex potest et debet eam sibi ⟨condecentem⟩ ⟨existimare⟩. Hec est ⟨summa⟩ ⟨eius⟩ quod in hac re ab Illustrissimo Principe meo retraere potui, qui, [?ut] ⟨uerum⟩ ⟨fatear⟩ [?Reuerendissime] Dominationi ⟨uestre⟩, ita liberaliter procedit et [?descendit] ad tam honestas condiciones ut neque ab Serenissimo Domino Rege uestro neque a ⟨uobis⟩ merito [?reiici] ⟨possint⟩; et eo minus quoniam plus in bonitate eius Excellentie quam in suma dotis reponere potestis, quoniam ipsa quemadmodum sangine ita et fortunam cum afinibus comunem habere solet. Translation english.md # DL 46150: English translation Maffeo da Treviglio, Milan, 30 November 1490, to Tamás Bakócz, bishop of Győr and chancellor of Hungary. Translated from reading/latin.md. The holes follow the Latin: [?word] = the Latin word rests on a suspect or unvalued sign (the sense is the one the context and the clear minute call for); [...] = not read; ⟨word⟩ = lost to damage in the cipher, filled from the clear minute. Words in round brackets are added for English sense. ## Summary Maffeo reports to Bakócz that he reached the Duke of Milan (Gian Galeazzo Sforza, "my Most Illustrious Prince") and set out what the bishop had done for the marriage alliance ("affinity") planned between the King of Hungary (the new king, Vladislas II) and the Duke, through the Duke's sister Bianca Maria Sforza, who had earlier been betrothed to John Corvinus, son of King Matthias. The Duke welcomes the alliance, now counts the bishop among his foremost friends, and sees it as the continuation of the bond made with King Matthias. The dowry asked by the King, said to exceed all measure, has given the Duke pause; still he will add to what he promised King Matthias: having once come down to 150,000 ducats, he now goes to 200,000, in jewels or money at the King's choice, with 10,000 of it for the bride's trousseau if paid in money, and the King to provide the jewels honourably. Bakócz is to send the courier back at once with the answer, and either have envoys sent with a mandate or have Milanese envoys come to conclude; otherwise he must report the new king's will and decision. ## Page 1 Not [?sooner] than the twentieth day [?of this] month was I able to reach my Most Illustrious Prince. To him, when the occasion offered, I faithfully set out the work done by Your Most Reverend [?Lordship] concerning the affinity that [?began] to be contracted between the Most Serene Lord King of Hungary and my aforesaid Most Illustrious Lord, by means of [...] [...] [...] (the Most Illustrious Lady Bianca), his sister; and how lately I was called to Buda on his behalf and introduced by her to the aforesaid Most Serene Lord King; and finally what was said and treated with me by her together with [...] [...] [...] [...] (the Magnificent Lord Chancellor of Bohemia), to whom the Most Serene Lord King had entrusted the matter to be handled. [?His] [?Excellency] [?received] [?it] [?gladly] and heard most willingly that the Most Serene Lord King is well disposed to contract an affinity with him. And since he learned from my words that Your Most Reverend Lordship too is most devoted to it, although he ought to incline to it chiefly for the benefit of [?the Most Serene] [...] [...] [...] [...] (Lord his King and) of the kingdom, ⟨yet⟩ not doubting that he [?will become] even more fervent towards it, with that [?most friendly] [?affection] which he has [?always] [?shown] to have had towards you, from the time when the affinity began to be treated with the late Most Serene King Matthias of happy memory until the present day: [?if] before he loved Your Most Reverend Lordship not moderately, now he has received you among his foremost and rare friends; and the more effectively your affection towards His Excellency has been proved by good works, the more increase has his love towards ## Page 2 you taken, of which he will without doubt reap the [?richest] [?fruit] [?whenever] time allows. The affinity of your Most Serene Lord King [...] is wonderfully welcome to my Most Illustrious Prince, because, besides the fact that His Excellency has always followed His Majesty with the highest love and goodwill, even before he ascended that throne, [?both] for his royal dignity and [?for] the singular goodness of his mind, since it was his intention to be joined with your kingdom through the affinity which he had contracted with King Matthias, [...] (and) that the Lord King himself was raised up by you, he will persuade himself, [?if] this affinity goes ahead, that he has continued what was begun before, not [?entered] into something new. It is true that the dowry sum [?asked] by His Majesty, [?as] it was seen to exceed measure, so it brought my Most Illustrious Prince into ⟨some⟩ [?hesitation]. For it seemed hard to him, as I too reminded Your Most Reverend Lordship, that such a sum should be asked of him as no king, however great, ever received in the name of dowry, nor does he [?see] from whom it could be had (the minute: "nay, let him see how it can be had by both"). But if His aforesaid Royal Majesty inclines to this affinity, as both she and you [?formerly] affirmed to me, the Excellency of my Prince will be content with some addition of dowry above what he once [?promised] [?King] Matthias, [?to show] that he wishes to have good regard both for the dignity of the house and for the nobility of her blood. ## Page 3 And [?as] he had before come down to one hundred and fifty thousand ducats, now he will extend himself to two hundred thousand, whether (the King) wishes to receive part of that [...] (sum) in [?jewels] or wishes to have money only: that will be left to the judgement of the Royal Majesty, [?except] that if he wants money only, he should know that out of the said [...] [...] [...] (sum of two hundred thousand) ten thousand must necessarily be spent on the clothing of the bride [...]; as for the jewels, the aforesaid Royal Majesty is to provide honourably [?according to] the dignity of both parties. And that sum, great as it is, any most worthy and most eminent king can and ought to ⟨think⟩ ⟨befitting⟩ for himself. This is ⟨the substance⟩ ⟨of what⟩ I could draw out of my Most Illustrious Prince in this matter, who, [?to] ⟨tell⟩ ⟨the truth⟩ to Your [?Most Reverend] Lordship, proceeds so liberally and [?comes down] to such honest [?conditions] that they cannot rightly be [?rejected] either by your Most Serene Lord King or by ⟨you⟩; and the less so because you can rest more on the goodness of His Excellency than on the dowry sum, since she is accustomed to have fortune, as blood, in common with her kinsmen by marriage. If His Majesty and you, as I hope, judge these conditions [?acceptable], Your Most Reverend Lordship will at once send back ⟨this⟩ courier with the [?answer], and either ## Page 4 will bring about that [...] envoys are sent without delay with a proper mandate, or will arrange that ours may come from here to you to conclude. If it turns out otherwise, (Your Lordship) must by all means inform me through the same courier of the will and decision of your Most Serene Lord King. In clear below the cipher: I commend myself from my heart to Your Most Reverend Lordship. Milan, on the feast of St Andrew the Apostle, "ult(im)a [?] decembris [?]" (so read; the feast and the minute give 30 November) 1490. Of Your Most Reverend Lordship the son, Maffeo da Treviglio. cardona1517.html

Two letters of the viceroy of Naples to the young Charles I of Spain, of 5 October 1517 and 18 June 1520 (BNE MSS/20210/11/1 and /4), each with passages in cipher and no decipherment on the pages. Michael Brackx recovered most of the key from the ciphertext alone, with Claude Code: letter signs and three-letter code groups that stand for whole words, in the family of Lannoy’s Naples cipher. Two names confirm it, Borghese Petrucci and Giampaolo Baglioni; about half the sentences still have holes, so it is decoded, not read. mok 63× que · tum 47× en · tue 45× de · fed 32× lo · mik 31× se de napoles a v de otubre de M.D.xvij Naples → the court of Charles I · letter signs and whole-word code groups · 5 October 1517 and 18 June 1520 · key recovered, text not read Ramón de Cardona to Charles I, Naples, 1517 and 1520 from Ramón de Cardona → to Charles V Go to the full text ↓ The viceroy of Naples writes to the young Charles in a nomenclator of letter signs and whole-word code groups. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) Contributed by Michael Brackx (solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · none (key obtained, text not read) The letters Ramón de Cardona, viceroy of Naples, to Charles I of Spain (emperor-elect from 1519). Two of the four letters bound together carry cipher: Naples, 5 October 1517, on the infantry in the kingdom and on the affairs of Rome and Siena, and Naples, 18 June 1520, on the proceedings in Rome and the pay of the troops. Where Madrid, Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/20210/11/1 and /4, in Cartas de Ramón de Cardona, Virrey de Nápoles (BNE Digital 0000173169, public domain). No decipherment on any page; no edition or study found. No DECODE record. The cipher An Aragonese-chancery nomenclator of the family of Charles de Lannoy’s Naples cipher: about 60 homophonic letter signs, some for letter pairs, and three-letter code groups that stand for whole words ( que , en , de , lo , el papa ). One table serves both letters. How the key was recovered By Michael Brackx with Claude Code, from the ciphertext alone: a joint annealer for sign and group values, given the class rule of Lannoy’s key and a list of whole-word options, then five rounds of fixing firm values and reading by context. Checks Matched and noisy controls on Lazarillo de Tormes ; a statistical test that passes; and two names that the key reads without having been built on them, Borghese Petrucci (1517) and Giampaolo Baglioni (1520). What it says The infantry cannot be kept or paid and the Pope is asked for money; Borghese Petrucci, brother of the executed cardinal, wishes to live and die under the Pope’s protection; in 1520 the proceedings after Giampaolo Baglioni’s beheading. About 75% of the plaintext letters read as sense; about half the sentences have no hole. Still open 22 code groups and five rare signs without a value, and three garbled runs; the published scan is about 1,070 px per page. Credit Michael Brackx ( issue #262 , pull request #264): transcription, key and reading, with Claude Code.

The BNE bound four letters from Naples to the Crown under one title. Two of them, MSS/20210/11/2 (2 March 1519) and /3 (24 December 1520), are wholly in clear. The other two carry cipher in separate passages inside clear text: part date cipher tokens /1 5 October 1517 (the BNE record says 5 March; the dateline reads a v de otubre de M D xvij ) block A (22 lines), block B (11 lines), block C (28 lines) 1,260 /4 18 June 1520 block D (19 lines, in two pieces) 403 The clear text around the blocks gives the setting: the 260 lances Cardona could not bring, the pay of the Count of Potenza’s men, the infantry that sacked Fabriano on its way to the kingdom, Don Ramón de Perellós sent to the ambassador Don Pedro de Urrea to ask the Pope for money para entretener la dicha ynfanteria ; in 1520 the defence against the Turkish fleet on the Apulian coast and houses to be built on the Monte di Gaeta. The start of block C in the 1517 letter. The clear text ends no sé lo que en esto se podrá acabar ; the cipher follows, fourteen lines (C01–C14) of letter signs and lower-case groups such as mok ( que ), tum ( en ), tue ( de ). The transcription has 1,663 tokens: 706 tokens of 115 three-letter code groups, 30 tokens of 11 two-letter groups ( mo , mj , fe …) and 927 sign tokens. Each cipher piece opens and closes with frame marks. The system is the family of Charles de Lannoy’s Naples cipher of 1522–27 as Olga Kolosova describes it ( El lenguaje secreto de la diplomacia de Carlos V , Valencia 2017, pp. 65–89), with its own table: Letter signs. A homophonic alphabet of about 60 types in use. Several stand for letter pairs: Lo is re , A is ll , x# is qu , and the capital E is rr , as in Lannoy’s table. Code groups. Three letters, consonant, vowel, consonant, with initials f g m n p r s t z; a few have two letters. They stand for whole words. The short ones are now and then also used as syllables ( par-la-me-nto ), but there are no syllable groups as in the 1511–15 Vich ciphers ( a different cipher, with its own page ); treating the groups as words is what made the solution possible. A class rule. From Lannoy’s key: the initial and the final letter of a group fix the first letter of its word, the vowel is free (here fed is lo and fid is la ). One table for both letters. 53 of the 67 code types in the 1520 letter also occur in the 1517 one. It is not Lannoy’s table: his values, such as tum for razón or fus for Milán , do not fit, and his letter values decode Cardona barely above chance. It is not the 1511–12 Vich table either. The BRAH 9/15 “Cifra del visorrey” (Galende Díaz 1994; DECODE R9815–R9820) was not compared, because its images need DECODE access.

Michael Brackx, working with Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) on 4 November 2026, used the joint annealer he built for the Vich letter of 1515 : every sign gets a letter or one of the 40 commonest letter pairs, every code group an entry from an option list or “unknown”, scored by a Spanish character five-gram plus the cost of the encipherment. The steps, including the ones that failed: step what result 1 Own solvers (letter n-gram annealing, code groups as words or syllables) and a control on vich1511 N.60 failed the scoring itself preferred wrong keys 2 The Vich annealer with its option list (words, syllables, letters), and a matched control ( Lazarillo at Cardona’s size) control: 99–100% of signs at 10M iterations; Cardona: top runs agree on at most about 75% of signs 3–4 A noisy control (35% of group values outside the list, 5.5% misreadings); tokenisation variants control best 2 of 16 runs at 90%; Cardona still did not converge 5 The same annealer with Lannoy’s class rule as a penalty ( wsa5.c ), on a structured noisy control 5 of 16 runs at 88–91% of signs 6 On Cardona, with the option list restricted to whole words worked top 6 runs agree on 85–94% of sign tokens; 35 of 63 sign types in 6 of 6 7 A chancery language model ( Celestina , Villa’s Memorias , the clear Vich letters; no Quijote ) with 34 signs fixed the frequent code groups agree: que, de, en, lo, se, el papa 8–11 Four more rounds: firm values fixed, the rest re-annealed (16–32 runs each), reading by context between rounds the remaining signs and about 60 more code types settled 12 A context pass over every stretch that decoded but did not read, sign by sign, with the class rule two signs and two groups overruled against unanimous runs, four groups read, two found to be nulls A value was fixed only when it read in every occurrence. The runs’ value was overruled where the image or every context disagreed: E is rr (the runs gave st ; they cannot produce rr ), A is ll ( si ) from Ballón , degollado and preuillegio , and ll is e ( on ) from recelo , terra , padre and vieren . The last two show that values all runs agree on can still be wrong where a sign is rare and its neighbours unsettled. The key is partial: firm probable doubtful open signs 54 4 1 5 code groups 78 14 12 22 Firm values are agreed by the runs or read by context in every occurrence; probable ones were 4–5 of 6 in an early run and not re-tested; doubtful ones are tentative context readings or model fillers, written [?word] . Each change is logged in the basis column of key/key.tsv .

Controls. A Lazarillo text enciphered the same way at Cardona’s size is recovered by the same annealer at 10M iterations; with a noisy option list and the class rule the structured control reaches 88–91% of signs in 5 of 16 runs. Cardona’s own runs agree at 85–94% once the options are whole words. Statistical validation ( docs/_validate.py , firm values only, 1,517 read tokens of 132 types): the reading scores −1.96 per letter on a Golden Age Spanish four-gram model, random keys of the same shape −3.40 (z 8.9), and a key annealed onto the shuffled ciphertext at best −2.37 (mean −2.40, z 17.7). Verdict: pass. Two names the key was not built on. 1517, block C: …lo que el papa esto le dize … al magnífico Burgès de Petrucis , Borghese Petrucci, former lord of Siena and brother of Cardinal Alfonso Petrucci, executed in the summer of 1517 for the plot against Leo X. 1520, block D: [Io]han Paulo Ballón and [Io]han Paulo, que a su padre han degollado , Giampaolo Baglioni, lord of Perugia, beheaded in Castel Sant’Angelo on Leo X’s order in June 1520; the phrase fits his sons. Clear text. Readings tie the cipher to the clear passage around it: entretener la dicha gente … pues que no tene con que pagarles against the clear entretener la dicha ynfanteria .

Code groups. 22 code types without a value and 12 doubtful, most occurring once or twice. The commonest open one is gie (3 tokens); others are probably names ( las cosas de nac y feg ); doubtful gnd ( mes ) reads in neither place. The candidate key is BRAH 9/15 ff. 1–6 (DECODE R9815–R9820), whose images need DECODE access. Rare signs. = , c# , 7+ , S , ^L# (1–7 tokens each); o+ may be two shapes (B09 prefers al ). At about 1,070 px per page several small signs are hard to separate, and no larger image is published. Garbled runs. A09 pedrona … rroarribare , C18 nuuosacredo , D07 ato…rondacreracho , and fax (5 tokens: esto in C16 but cardenales in D03 and A11, perhaps two groups confused). The published scan is the largest available; a recheck needs a better image from the BNE. Doubtful readings. A = ll and ll = e are probable (grade I, by context); zes and sim are probably nulls; mel mando , toq da and tud dar are tentative (I).
