Filippo Sega, Bishop of Piacenza, wrote from Paris to Rome in 1590–91; his despatches are in the Segreteria di Stato, Francia 32. The first letter was written in Paris at the end of November 1590, just after the siege had been lifted by Farnese. In the clear text before the cipher Sega speaks of a bishop kept in prison, of a “sacrilege” that stirs the city and of requests for his release; the cipher holds his own judgement. The second letter is addressed to Cardinal Caetani and speaks of Mayenne, the Duke of Bavaria and Sega’s own affairs at Rome. A faint note at the head of f. 71r, “… Decifrata 17 …”, shows that a contemporary decipherment once existed; it is not among the images on DECODE. F. 17r. The clear text ends with et si fa instanza per rimedi della rilassatione ; the cipher begins on the same line with 28 32 41 25 38 32 35 28 23 3^ , io et fuori de . A mark in the left margin precedes the passage. The signs over the digits are what separates one vowel from another. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 32 f. 17r, via DECODE R5612.
sega1590.html#cipher

Meister printed the key in 1906 ( Die Geheimschrift im Dienste der päpstlichen Kurie , no. 65, pp. 435–436). A two-digit number is a letter or a syllable (28 i, 31 n, 35 r, 37 t, 42 a, 24 e). A sign over a digit gives the vowel: a diaeresis a, a circumflex e, a bar i, a cross o, a small 2 u. Single letters stand for words ( Z non, c per, b che, l il, X della), a few symbols for tanto , quanto , in , ma , più , and dotted three-digit numbers for names (128 Mayenne, 129 Navarre, 453 Villeroy). The digits 7, 8, 9 and 0 are nulls. The key is in targets/sega1590/key.tsv .

The key. George Lasry identified key no. 65 for Sega’s letter of 9 January 1591 (BnF Français 3613), a separate target . Brice Dudout recognised the same cipher on f. 17r, where the word Villeroy is written over the number 453 in the DECODE image, and applied the key without changing a value. The test. A protocol was written and hashed before any calculation. Sega’s letter of 21 December 1590 (Francia 32 ff. 228v and 231; DECODE R5621) carries a contemporary decipherment on f. 230, dated 26 March 1591. The decipherment was transcribed and frozen first; the cipher was then decoded with key 65 unchanged. 268 of 287 characters (0.934) and 56 of 65 words (0.862) agree, against at most 0.551 and 0.492 for 200 controls with the letter values permuted. The criteria, 0.85 and 0.75, were met. The caveat is Brice Dudout’s: the transcriptions were made with the key in mind. A letter of 2 July 1591 (R5618) is in another system; key 65 segments only 62.5% of its pairs, under the 85% threshold fixed beforehand, and was rejected there. The letters. The passage of 26 November 1590 (345 signs) and the groups of 16 January 1591 were transcribed from the images, frozen, decoded with key 65 and read. A third letter of Sega, the duplicate of early January 1591 (R5615), was decoded with the same key and read only in part; it is not part of this entry.

I myself, and outside the parties, have some information on the bishop’s bad nature and his leaning towards the opposite party, not so much for reasons of modern politics as from a limping religion. I shall go on temporising as much as I can, making outward shows of feeling for and against him, but slow in execution, meanwhile stirring the parties to spew out all they know and can, [in clear: so as to be able to inform Rome better and resolve more maturely what is fitting in so notable an incident.] The last enciphered sentence is obscure and is not translated. The cipher of the first letter has no et before anderò ; the established text of the contributor adds it. In the second letter (16 January 1591) the enciphered words are set inside Sega’s clear sentences, which the contributor gives abridged. Sega says the Duke of Mayenne (128) told the provincial that he had written to Rome something good for him, but so obscurely that Sega does not understand it; that he needs with the Pope no stronger intercession than the one the Duke of Bavaria offers of his own motion; and that he has awaited “quel pomo” with singular patience and dissimulation for many years. The contributor’s hypothesis, which is not established here, is that the fruit is the red hat: Sega was made cardinal in December 1591. Translation translation.md # English translation I myself, and outside the parties, have some information on the bishop's bad nature and his leaning towards the opposite party, not so much for reasons of modern politics as from a limping religion. I shall go on temporising as much as I can, making outward shows of feeling for and against him, but slow in execution, meanwhile stirring the parties to spew out all they know and can, [in clear:] so as to be able to inform [Rome] better and resolve more maturely what is fitting in so notable an incident. The last enciphered sentence ("<canonizatorio> della festa ... se non è più che caduto") remains obscure and is not translated. ## Second letter: Paris, 16 January 1591 (f. 71r-v) [f. 71r] ... and what I wrote to you of having discussed with Mayenne about the service of the Pope, I did not think it necessary to have it sent in duplicate ... He wrote to His Holiness ... without even mentioning you, despite my first advice, already approved as good by His Excellency himself: a proof of the reading he makes ... and of the application of his mind to affairs; but let it pass. The provincial wrote to me that Mayenne himself told him he had written something or other good for me to Rome; but he writes it so obscurely that I do not understand it exactly ... What Mayenne wrote, I do not know. ... not finding that I need, with the Pope, a greater, more powerful and more timely intercession than the one which the lord Duke of Bavaria, of his own motion and as a good father, takes under his protection, and which I promise myself, in due time and place, in the favour of His Highness ... [f. 71v] ... that fruit ("quel pomo") whose proper season I have awaited with singular patience and dissimulation for so many years ... the freedom to speak the truth, which this cause particularly needs, represented as it is by both sides far from what it really is. Translation translation.md # English translation I myself, and outside the parties, have some information on the bishop's bad nature and his leaning towards the opposite party, not so much for reasons of modern politics as from a limping religion. I shall go on temporising as much as I can, making outward shows of feeling for and against him, but slow in execution, meanwhile stirring the parties to spew out all they know and can, [in clear:] so as to be able to inform [Rome] better and resolve more maturely what is fitting in so notable an incident. The last enciphered sentence ("<canonizatorio> della festa ... se non è più che caduto") remains obscure and is not translated. ## Second letter: Paris, 16 January 1591 (f. 71r-v) [f. 71r] ... and what I wrote to you of having discussed with Mayenne about the service of the Pope, I did not think it necessary to have it sent in duplicate ... He wrote to His Holiness ... without even mentioning you, despite my first advice, already approved as good by His Excellency himself: a proof of the reading he makes ... and of the application of his mind to affairs; but let it pass. The provincial wrote to me that Mayenne himself told him he had written something or other good for me to Rome; but he writes it so obscurely that I do not understand it exactly ... What Mayenne wrote, I do not know. ... not finding that I need, with the Pope, a greater, more powerful and more timely intercession than the one which the lord Duke of Bavaria, of his own motion and as a good father, takes under his protection, and which I promise myself, in due time and place, in the favour of His Highness ... [f. 71v] ... that fruit ("quel pomo") whose proper season I have awaited with singular patience and dissimulation for so many years ... the freedom to speak the truth, which this cause particularly needs, represented as it is by both sides far from what it really is. Three letters of Henry of Navarre to his envoy raising a German army (BnF 500 Colbert 401), listed by Tomokiyo among unsolved ciphers. The key, a homophonic alphabet and a syllable table both in alphabetical order, was recovered from the ciphertext alone by a solver built on that design and checked on matched controls; the three letters are decrypted, with a dozen word signs open. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 16 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete Credits · George Lasry (unpublished earlier solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letters Three letters of 1585–86 from Henry of Navarre to Ségur, who was negotiating with the German princes. They press him to conclude with Duke John Casimir, raise the largest levy possible and march it at once; the 1583 letter at f. 143 is a letter to Ségur. Where BnF, Cinq cents de Colbert 401, ff. 233, 239 and 288v (f. 143 also in figures); Gallica ark:/12148/btv1b10035574w. The cipher 461 figures over 102 distinct values: an alphabetical syllable table in blocks of five ( ba be bi bo bu …), letters, doubles, nulls, and a few word-signs written in letters. How it was read The blocks-of-five structure was found first. An annealer with the letters’ clear French as context gave a key that came out alphabetical by itself; the same method recovers 97% of a matched control. What it says Clervant is to raise two thousand reiters and ten thousand écus; Navarre asks which road the army will take, the Vivarais or Dauphiné; in April 1586 he confesses “extreme anxiety” at having no news. Credit S. Tomokiyo’s page lists the four letters and the different key he reconstructed from the interlinear decipherment at f. 321. Still open A dozen word-signs written in letters (pi, na, gne, H, L…) and three nomenclature numbers are glossed from context or left open. The 1583 letter at f. 143 is in another key and is not deciphered.

The 1583 letter at f. 143 turned out to be to Ségur, from a correspondent at Beaupréau, and its clear text describes the system: “vous y avez toutes choses tellement dispersées en lettres, syllabes, doubles, nulles et tout le reste qu’il est impossible de le descouvrir … Les noms sont en lettres et syllabes.” Letters, syllables, doubles, nulls, and names written with letter-signs: that is exactly what the 1585–86 key proves to be. The 1583 letter itself is in a different key, not deciphered: a different cipher, with its own page .

Two ranges. Values 1–53 carry 311 tokens, 54–123 carry 146, and only three exceed 123. Counting the upper range by residue mod 5 gives 60 · 30 · 22 · 20 · 14 for one alignment and near-flat counts for the other four: blocks of five with one dominant position, which is what an alphabetical syllabary ( a e i o u , e commonest) produces. The structure was fixed before a single letter was known. A structured annealer. Each number below the table is a free homophone (22 letters or a null, nulls capped); each block of five is one consonant with the vowel given by position; letter-glyphs are skipped; and the clear French around every cipher passage is kept as fixed context for a 16th-century French 5-gram model (Catherine de Médicis’ letters, Teulet, Labanoff; 9.4 M letters). Moves reassign or swap letter symbols and block consonants. Five of twelve seeds converged on one key. Controls. Passages of Catherine de Médicis enciphered with random keys of the same shape, the same token counts and the same interleaving of clear text. With the table start guessed at 64 the method recovered one control at 90 % and one at 47 %; with the true structure (start 54, fourteen consonants) it recovers a control at 96.6 % of letter tokens and 12 of 14 blocks , missing only x and f at one token each. The blind key was already alphabetical. Without being told so, the annealer put a at 4–6, b at 7, c at 9–10, d at 11–12, e at 13–15, g at 18, h at 20–21, i at 22–24, l at 26, m at 27–28, n at 29–30, o at 31, p at 34–35, r at 38–39, s at 40–42, t at 43–44 and u at 45–47. Against the final key it had 86 % of the letter tokens and 77 % of the syllables right even with the table start wrong by two blocks. The decryption gave capituler et conclure promptement avec ceux que vous adviserez … le duc Casimir … faire la levée … la faire marcher … deux mille reistres … dix mil escus … Vivarès ou Daulphiné directly. Context fixed the rest. et conclure = 52 62 29 9 83 105 , secours = 110 62 46 39 42 and le duc Casimir = 80 68 9 59 111 86 38 force 62 = co , 59 = ca , 65 = de ; bien = 56 14 29 gives 56 = bi : the table begins at 54 with b c d f g l m n p q r s t v . que vous and qu’il fix 99–103 = qua que qui … ; Clervant fixes 119 = va ; nece□aire makes the square ss , mi2e makes 2 = ll , lev1 makes 1 = ée ; 52 = et , 53 a null. The rest of the volume, and f. 366 (added later on 16 September 2026) All 440 canvases of the volume were fetched and examined on contact sheets. Cipher occurs on six leaves only: the four above, Tomokiyo’s ff. 321 and 333, and one leaf not on his list, f. 366 , an autograph of Navarre to Ségur from the autumn of 1586 ( on a fait avancer l’armée et les forces contre moy … d’user de toute la diligence que vous pourrez pour effectuer ce dont je vous ay chargé ) with three short cipher lines at its foot. Its low figures and a letter-written sign gu put it in the ff. 233 key; the last line decrypts as escri , the first two ( ri-e-c-h-a-v-f-fe-n , re-de-du-pi-n gu la-que ) look like names in the king’s own spelling and are left open. There is no further secretary letter in this key in the volume, so the word-signs stay unglossed. Nine other letters of Navarre in the volume are in clear. The two leaves Tomokiyo lists under Henry III, ff. 321 and 333, are Navarre’s too, but in the key Tomokiyo rebuilt from the f. 321 interlinear decipherment: the same chancery design with the letters shifted by eight. f. 333 (La Rochelle, 10 July 1586) was decrypted with that key and is a different cipher, with its own page . f. 366 is left here as probably this key, open ; it is not counted among the letters deciphered.

Jacques de Ségur-Pardaillan was Navarre’s agent in England, Denmark and the Empire from 1583, and Claude-Antoine de Vienne, sieur de Clervant, his colleague for the German levy; Duke John Casimir of the Palatinate was the prince through whom Huguenot armies of reiters had been raised since 1567. Navarre’s October 1585 letter follows the bull of 9 September excommunicating him and the summer campaign that cost him most of his Guyenne places; the “contract with the Churches” and Clervant’s two thousand reiters refer to the standing obligation under which the Huguenot assemblies financed the German horse, and the ten thousand écus from [180] is most naturally the English subsidy (an inference, not a decryption). The February and April 1586 letters belong to the long wait for the army that was finally assembled in 1587 under the baron of Dohna and destroyed at Auneau. The postscript’s Drak is Drake’s West Indies voyage: Santo Domingo fell on 1 January 1586, and the news reached France in February.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) · On the map ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · none (key obtained, text not read) The letter Sienese envoys on a journey to the “Magnificis et potentibus dominis Prioribus [et] Capitaneo Civitatis Senarum”; signed by one ending “Marco”, perhaps at Rome; undated, before 1429. Where Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2, no. 14; DECODE R4802, catalogued “1500–1599” with no status. The cipher Italian, one sign per letter with a few extra signs for e, o, i and a, word points kept, and code signs for persons and a number (<7H>, <Z7>, (420)). How it was deciphered A plain search stuck; three hand cribs on repeated words found the key, and the staged annealing search later reached the same key with no crib. What it says The envoys report a two-hour talk with a servant of <7H> and the “gielosia” of Carlo Malatesta and others; Tuscany might join “the three powers” in open war on <Z7>. Still open The letter as a text: 436 signs in doubtful words, 161 unread, the codes, and the date. The reading audit of 22 October 2026 kept lines 1–6 as read; checked on 23 October with every doubtful word counted as a hole, they too fail (no clean sentence), so the whole page is decoded, not read. This letter was filed on this site until 14 October 2026 with the rest of the Sienese bundle of cipher letters, in which each letter has its own key. The other letters whose keys were found are different ciphers, each with its own page: no. 25 , no. 18 , no. 4 (Borghesi, 1456) and nos. 6 and 24 (deciphered by George Lasry); the unread pieces, including Meister’s unphotographed no. 1 of 1421, are on the bundle’s page .

A whole page in cipher, 23 lines and a subscription: 1,495 signs in words divided by points. A plain annealing search stuck on pseudo-Italian; three hand cribs on repeated words ( vostra , stato ) found the key, and the staged search later reached the same key with no crib. Reading it on the image split two glyphs the first transcription had merged (an o with a stroke in from the left is m , with a stroke out to the right d ) and two more (a compact 8 is v , a tall looped one n ). 876 of 1,495 signs (58.6%) are in words read as sense , 436 (29.2%) in words with a doubtful letter, 161 (10.8%) unread, and 22 are code signs. No. 14, the opening lines: … per la gracia di dio noi arivamo qui [h]ieri da sera … Image: Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 14, via DECODE R4802.
siena14.html#reading

… per la gracia di dio noi arivamo qui [h]ieri da sera salvi e […] la nostra compa(n)gnia … significhiamo a la Signoria vostra come questa matina, trovandosi Domenico con uno servidore di <7H> […] a ragionare per spacio da ore due … ancora afferma l’amico vostro che Carlo [M]alatesti e ogni altro sono in questa medesima gielosia … L’Altissimo acresca e conservi la magnifica Signoria vostra, a la quale umilmente ci racomandiamo. This is a partial reading: most of its words rest on look-alike sign classes (Q/Q4, 8/TH, P/PHI; a/i, u/n, o/i) that the DECODE image, at about 15–20 pixels a sign, does not separate, so the sense below is a gist and the letter counts as decoded, not read. The envoys arrived “yesterday evening” with their company. Domenico spent two hours with a servant of a lord written <7H>, who is displeased with an enterprise “given by <Z7> to (420)”; Carlo Malatesta and the others share the same jealousy; they think Siena and the rest of Tuscany, united with “the three powers”, could openly make war on <Z7>; <7H> is in the field and may yet come to terms. The subscription seems to read Rome (a clear-text “roma” with a tick, uncertain) as the place of writing, with a signatory ending “Marco” (also uncertain). Carlo Malatesta of Rimini died in 1429 , so the letter is no later; the wars of 1409–14 and 1423–24 are the candidates. It is the one piece in the bundle that could be close to Meister’s no. 1 of 1421, but it carries no date and 1421 cannot be claimed for it.

The articles Maximilian I put to the Sienese orators at Pisa in November 1496, subscribed by his secretary Niklas Ziegler, with every sensitive word in cipher (Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 18, DECODE R4806). The cipher Homophonic substitution on 60 signs: letter signs with homophones, signs for doubled letters (rr, pp, ss, ll, cc, tt), dotted or barred signs as nulls, and a few code capitals (B., X., M.X.) left in clear. How it was deciphered Twice from the ciphertext alone. Here on 24 September 2026 (annealing with a Latin model, 87.1% read); independently by George Lasry with CTTS and Claude on 15–17 October 2026, from cribs in the clear Latin around the cipher words. His key agrees with ours on 35 of his 38 letter signs. What it says Siena is to join the Holy League at half the Pope’s quota, lend the King 5,000 ducats, ready its artillery and open war on the enemy at Ponte a Valiano; the orators ask for every place taken within five miles of their border. Three written pages (P4, P3, P1 in DECODE’s numbering; P2 is blank) carry 1,469 cipher signs in point-separated words inside the running Latin, by George Lasry’s count. P4 opens “Primo loco petita per Cesaream Maiestatem ab oratoribus Senensibus”; P1 carries the subscription “Niccolaus Ziegler, Regis Secretarius” and the King’s second demands. The project’s key (24 September 2026) came from the annealing search with a Latin model on a transcription of 30 sign names; a check on the images split three look-alike pairs and showed that dotted signs are nulls. It read 1,271 of 1,459 signs (87.1%). George Lasry’s key, recovered without ours, names 60 signs, because his transcription separates glyphs ours had merged. Matched sign by sign, 35 of his 38 letter and doubled-letter signs carry the same value in ours (3 of them as glyphs our transcription had merged with a look-alike); one differs (a sign he reads cc , we c ), and two signs that occur once each are not in ours. The one passage printed on his web page ( restituerentur, ita tamen quod ipsi Senenses … stare iuri coram ) is our own reading of it word for word, cipher and clear words falling the same way. siena18.html#reading

George Lasry’s reading, quoted from his report; abbreviations expanded in square brackets, the code capitals in brackets, ÷ and ✱ single unread signs. The full Latin and translation are in lasry_report.md . Item q[uod] pro bono rei p[ublice] Sen[ensis] ÷ et [B]. illico manus apponerent ut saltem medietas illor[um] castrorum et arcium, ad que ipsi Senensib[us] ius competit, eis restituerentur, ita t[ame]n q[uod] ipsi Senenses ad requisitionem Florentinorum sint contenti de stando iuri coram Cesare, dummodo Florentini etiam de illis que ipsi occupant sint contenti stare iuri coram ÷ “That, for the good of the Sienese republic, [the League] should at once put its hand to it, so that at least half of the castles and fortresses to which the Sienese have a right are restored to them; on condition that the Sienese, at the Florentines’ request, be content to stand to law before Caesar, provided that the Florentines likewise be content to stand to law before [Caesar] over the places they occupy.” (his translation) P4, the King’s first demands. Siena is to state its grievances against Florence and the places the Florentines hold; accept Caesar as ordinary and supreme judge; join the Most Holy League at a quota set by Caesar, half the Pope’s; and supply passage, victuals, 100 men-at-arms and 60 light horse. P3, the Sienese counter-demands. Every town, fortress and castle within five miles of the Sienese border taken in the war goes to Siena, and the “diligentia” and the tower at the Valiano bridge are to be handed over before any peace with the enemy. P1, the King’s second demands. Talamone and the artillery are to be put in order; Siena lends the King 5,000 ducats, which [M.X.] will repay within two months; Siena enters the League, which will protect its present regime, and opens war on the enemy around Ponte a Valiano. Subscribed by Niklas Ziegler. Date. The articles are undated. George Lasry places them at Pisa in November 1496, during Maximilian I’s Italian expedition with the forces of the Holy League of 1495, whose treaty set the Pope’s quota at half the others’: Ziegler is attested as the King’s secretary from 1494 and was with the court on 25 November 1496 (Regesta Imperii XIV,2 n. 4508), Pecci’s Balìa deliberations of September–October 1496 record the same demands, and the Sienese attacks on the Florentine bastion at Ponte a Valiano in 1496 were made at the League’s urging (Guicciardini III.8). This page earlier gave “1510s–1520s”; his dating replaces it.

His reading covers the words ours left open or doubtful. Graded against our transcription and key (H read from the key, M uncertain), in ten places (eleven words, ponant and pulveres sharing one place) his readings are H: in ordinem (where we saw a struck word), ponant , pulveres , que after B., cum , armature , defendat (ours defendam ), quote (ours quoti ), imponitur , ius competit , habeat ; three are M: Telamonem (the damaged first word), pax (ours passo? ) and his own query s[anctissima]? . In six places of the clear Latin his readings are the grammatical ones. The table, sign by sign and word by word, is in lasry_comparison.md . The statistical test on the project’s own key ( docs/_validate.py , Latin letter model) gave underdetermined : our transcription kept look-alike pairs under one sign name, so a one-value-per-sign key scored below the annealer. George Lasry’s key, which separates those glyphs, explains why.

WHAT IT IS: Latin articles/petitions ("Item quod ...", "Secundo loco petit ...", "petita ab oratoribus Senensibus"), i.e. a negotiated text between Siena and a royal/imperial chancery, with the substantive words written in cipher in the running text. Word-divided: cipher words are separated by a point (" · ") or space, exactly like the clear words, so each cipher group is one plaintext word. - P1: end of a first set of articles, signed "Niccolo Zieglog(?)(r.) Regis Secretarius ss." (subscription in the same hand: probably Niklas Ziegler, secretary of Maximilian I / Charles V as King, i.e. before 1520/21?; the reading of the surname is uncertain) -- then "Secundo loco petit [..] Ce(saree) M(aiesta)ti //" and articles. - P2: verso, blank (only bleed-through of P1/P3 visible). - P3: articles continued; heading "petita ab oratoribus Senensibus". - P4: heading "[..] loco petita per Ce(saream) M(aiesta)tem ab oratoribus Senensibus"; pencil folio no. "18" at the foot. No date, no address found on the four images. Hand: one scribe for clear and cipher, brown ink. Contains the clear words "Ser.mo d(omino) Regi", "Ce. M.tas", "Senenses", "d(omi)ni Senenses", "B.", "X.", "Mx." -- B., X. and Mx. stand alone between points and look like abbreviations/code letters, not cipher words. SIGN LEGEND (the cipher is a set of ~30 simple pen signs, most of them letter- or digit-like) N square-topped n, "П" (bar with two legs) n round-topped n, "∩" (smaller, round head; distinct from N where legible; merge if in doubt) U u, "ᴜ" (two uprights joined at the foot) + plus / cross W "ш" (three uprights on a foot bar) o small o; often written with a lead-in stroke from the left ("-o"); the stroke is ignored c c D reversed c, "ɔ" Y γ / y (V-fork with a curved tail below the line) h h-like sign with the right leg descending in a tail ("ɧ") HX h crossed by a long slanting stroke (looks like a deletion, but recurs, so kept as a sign) H capital H (often with a dot above "Ḣ") T "⊣": horizontal stroke from the left meeting an upright (like -|) L "⊢": upright with a stroke to the right (|-), also "r"-like F "Γ" / "ſ": tall upright with a hook/bar to the right at the top S "ʃ"/"ς": slanting s-curve descending below the line Q q-like: bowl on the left, stem on the right going through above and below ("ɖ"/"ф") 4 figure 4 with a descender (open 4) 9 figure 9 / g: bowl with a long slanting descender 3 ʒ (figure 3 with the tail below the line) 6 figure 6 7 figure 7 (angular "ᒣ") 8 figure 8 OO "∞" (two joined loops), also written "ao" PX upright crossed by a star/asterisk-like stroke (✱ on a stem); may be clear "pro/per" abbreviation - a dash inside a word ENTRIES: clear text in [ ]; cipher words separated by " · " as on the page; signs inside a word by spaces. Contents From: Maximilian I, King of the Romans (royal chancery; subscribed by the secretary Niklas Ziegler) To: the orators of Siena (with their counter-demands) Place: Pisa Date: November 1496 — undated; fixed by Maximilian’s stay at Pisa, Ziegler’s secretaryship and the Valiano fighting (see context) A record of a negotiation in three parts. The King’s first demands (P4): Siena is to state its grievances against Florence and the places the Florentines hold, accept Caesar as supreme judge, join the Most Holy League at a quota set by Caesar (half the Pope’s), and supply passage, victuals, 100 men-at-arms and 60 light horse. The Sienese counter-demands (P3): places taken within five miles of Siena’s borders go to Siena, and the “diligentia” and the tower at the Valiano bridge are handed over before any peace with the enemy. The King’s second demands (P1): Talamone and the artillery to be put in order, a loan of 5,000 ducats to the King repayable in two months, Siena to enter the League, which will protect its present regime, and to open war on the enemy around Ponte a Valiano; subscribed by the royal secretary Niklas Ziegler. Historical context and dating The articles belong to Maximilian I’s Italian expedition of autumn 1496, when the King of the Romans lay at Pisa and before Livorno with the forces of the Holy League of 1495 (whose treaty set the Pope’s quota at half the other members’) and summoned Siena to join the war on Florence. Niklas Ziegler is attested as his secretary from 1494 and was with the court on the Pontremoli pass on 25 November 1496 [Regesta Imperii XIV,2 n. 4508]; Maximilian signed “Maximilianus rex” at Pisa on 13 November 1496 while Italians called him “la cesarea maestà” [RI XIV,2 n. 4485; Sanudo, Diarii I]; Pecci’s Balìa deliberations of September–October 1496 record the same demands (orators to the King, bombards shipped from Talamone to Livorno, men-at- arms, no accord with Florence) [Pecci, Memorie storico-critiche]; and the Sienese attacks on the Florentine bastion at the Ponte a Valiano in 1496 were made at the League’s urging [Guicciardini, Storia d’Italia III.8]. The DECODE date “1500–1599” is a placeholder. Open points. The code [M.X.] — a full-quota League member guaranteeing the loan, the King himself or Milan — is unidentified. The full decryption and translation follow at the end of this section. Contents From: Maximilian I, King of the Romans (royal chancery; subscribed by the secretary Niklas Ziegler) To: the orators of Siena (with their counter-demands) Place: Pisa Date: November 1496 — undated; fixed by Maximilian’s stay at Pisa, Ziegler’s secretaryship and the Valiano fighting (see context) A record of a negotiation in three parts. The King’s first demands (P4): Siena is to state its grievances against Florence and the places the Florentines hold, accept Caesar as supreme judge, join the Most Holy League at a quota set by Caesar (half the Pope’s), and supply passage, victuals, 100 men-at-arms and 60 light horse. The Sienese counter-demands (P3): places taken within five miles of Siena’s borders go to Siena, and the “diligentia” and the tower at the Valiano bridge are handed over before any peace with the enemy. The King’s second demands (P1): Talamone and the artillery to be put in order, a loan of 5,000 ducats to the King repayable in two months, Siena to enter the League, which will protect its present regime, and to open war on the enemy around Ponte a Valiano; subscribed by the royal secretary Niklas Ziegler. Historical context and dating The articles belong to Maximilian I’s Italian expedition of autumn 1496, when the King of the Romans lay at Pisa and before Livorno with the forces of the Holy League of 1495 (whose treaty set the Pope’s quota at half the other members’) and summoned Siena to join the war on Florence. Niklas Ziegler is attested as his secretary from 1494 and was with the court on the Pontremoli pass on 25 November 1496 [Regesta Imperii XIV,2 n. 4508]; Maximilian signed “Maximilianus rex” at Pisa on 13 November 1496 while Italians called him “la cesarea maestà” [RI XIV,2 n. 4485; Sanudo, Diarii I]; Pecci’s Balìa deliberations of September–October 1496 record the same demands (orators to the King, bombards shipped from Talamone to Livorno, men-at- arms, no accord with Florence) [Pecci, Memorie storico-critiche]; and the Sienese attacks on the Florentine bastion at the Ponte a Valiano in 1496 were made at the League’s urging [Guicciardini, Storia d’Italia III.8]. The DECODE date “1500–1599” is a placeholder. Open points. The code [M.X.] — a full-quota League member guaranteeing the loan, the King himself or Milan — is unidentified. siena19.html#letter

The clear part, six and a half lines in a fast cursive, says that since their last letter of the 6th, sent by a messenger of their own, the envoys have been several times with the S. Capitano and pressed for their departure; he answers that, since they are there, they can wait until he has a reply, which will come very soon, and he said so all of yesterday, “che fumo di octo al presente di marzo”. So the letter was written on 9 March; no year and no place are given, and the letter ends in cipher without a signature. George Lasry dates it to the 1440s; his report does not give the grounds. The end of the letter: “domattina partiamo col nome di dio”, then the cipher, with the clear phrases “e in effecto afferma”, “per ogni modo e l’altro”, “che venne” and “se altro non nascera” between the runs. The catalogue had five DECODE records of “Lord Threr? to unknown recipient”, 1592–94, marked Non-decrypted (no decipherment known). There is a sixth, R7771, in the same run. They are letters to the Lord Treasurer, Burghley, among the papers of Thomas Edmondes, Elizabeth’s agent with Henri IV. The writer reports what the King told him in person, and dates from Tours, Blois and the camp before Laon. In each letter a few lines are written in invented symbols inside the clear English. The cipher is a simple substitution of English, keeping word divisions, with a few homophones and single symbols for persons. The key was recovered from the ciphertext alone by taking frequent cipher words as the , of and to , and the same key serves all six letters, in two hands. Every passage is deciphered, 1,023 of the 1,035 cipher signs (98.8%); the last, four lines on f. 59, on 2 October 2026, with one new sign. The twelve signs not read are the person symbols and one unexplained sign. The passages include the King breaking off his sister’s marriage to [Soissons?], Montmorency’s demand for custody of the young Prince of Condé, a would-be purchaser told “that his faith is not vendible”, and [Guise?]’s designs on Champagne and Reims in 1594. Butler’s Edmondes Papers (1913) prints five of the six letters with the cipher deciphered. That was found only after the key had been recovered here, so this break is an independent re-solution. The letter on ff. 109–110 is the one Butler leaves out. Stowe MS 166 f. 50 (R7770): “as it pleaseth himself to tell me) as especiallye”, then six lines of cipher, “to breake of the marriage betwene her and [9]…” Image: British Library, Stowe MS 166 f. 50, via DECODE R7770.

DECODE ff. date cipher R7770 50–51 [Chartres, 19 January 1592/3] 6 lines R7771 56–57 Tours, 16 February 1592/3 4 lines R7772 58–59 Tours, 3 March 1592/3 6 + 4 lines R7773 60–61 Blois, 16 March 1592/3 2 lines R7774 109–110 camp before Laon, July 1594 10 lines R7775 111–112 [camp before Laon, 23 July 1594] 3 lines Edmondes wrote the English year, which began on 25 March, so the letters dated January to March 1592 belong to 1593 in modern reckoning. Butler prints them under 1593, and the bracketed dates are his. The DECODE “sender” fields (John le Rios, John Symmons, “Permell of Dieppo”, “One of Dieppe”) come from endorsements. The letters themselves are written by someone at the King’s side, in Edmondes’s papers.

A = δ, b = +, c = 2, d = ш, e = ʋ, f = 8, g = б/6, h = 4, i = ǂ, k = 7, l = 3, m = □, n = ȝ, o = α, p = 9, r = f, s = &, t = ω, u/v = ш or a small o, w = π, x = 5, y = λ. ш serves for d as well as u/v, and б for a as well as g. Code symbols for persons: 9 standing alone (probably the Count of Soissons, 1593); n (a suitor for Catherine de Bourbon; Love (2001), quoting the same sentence from the letter as Burghley received it, glosses him as the Duke of Montpensier (M)); £ , £2 (probably the Duke of Guise, 1594); o , a small circle, twice on f. 109v (by context the King, I). Eleven occurrences in all.

f. 50 (R7770). “…the K. continueth his resolution to goe to Saumur to see his sister, not so much for that cause (as it pleaseth himself to tell me) as especiallye to breake of the marriage betwene her and [9] wch he tould me he is resolued not to permitt but to geive her vnto [n] of whom he said he hath great hope that he will render himself of the religion. [9] is herewth enraged and extreemelie discontented .” f. 57 (R7771). “…by the Pope, will appeare vnto yor L. by the enclosed. [9]: is glad to here of, hoping to be no further troubled wth the clamor of the Catholikes for the seekinge of him .” f. 58v (R7772). “ I doe secretelie learne that Monsr Montmorancy hath made great instance, as a condition whereof he required the performance before he would come, to haue the yong prince of Condé deliuered into the handes of Madame d’Angolesme his sister in law to be vnder his custodie .” f. 59 (R7772), deciphered 2 October 2026. The four cipher lines at the head of f. 59 continue that sentence: “ and by consequence popis[h]lie nourished, pretending so to appertaine to the place of the Constable, to haue the gouer[n]ment of the younge heire of the crowne , but wherein he hath nothing effected, the K. being resolued not to assent thereunto.” The young heir of the crown is the Prince of Condé of f. 58v. They were transcribed from the full-resolution DECODE image and read with the key unchanged, 126 signs for 126 letters, except for one sign that occurs only here, a vertical stroke for q in consequence . The fragments recorded before, “papistes” and an “effected” in cipher, were misreadings: the cipher word is popislie , and effected is in the clear ending. All twenty distinct words of the decipherment stand, in Butler’s modern spelling ( popishly , appertain , government ), on his p. 56 in the HathiTrust word data, against ten on the next best page of the volume; his page text itself could not be opened. f. 59 (R7772): and by consequence popislie nourished pretending / so to appertaine to the place of the constable / to haue the gouerment of the younge heire of / the crowne , then in clear “but wherein he hath nothing effected, the K. being resolued not to assent thereunto”. The vertical stroke in the first line is q . Who the person symbols stand for. 9 = Soissons and £ = Guise fit the context (M); n is the Duke of Montpensier in Love’s gloss (M). o, twice on f. 109v, is by context the King (I). No key with names survives: Tomokiyo’s Elizabethan tables have no Edmondes cipher, Unton’s cypher of 1591 is a different system, and DECODE has no Edmondes key record (checked 2 October 2026); HMC Salisbury IV and Birch (1749) print no decipherment naming them, and the Calendar of State Papers Foreign for 1592–94 is not online. F. 59 has no person sign. These eleven signs and the “3:” of f. 109v are the twelve of 1,035 not read. The new sign on f. 59, a vertical stroke for q , occurs once (C). The sign “3:” before the said townes on f. 109v (after the clear “by the meanes of the duke”) is not explained. “Hope” and “marriage” on f. 50 are under blots (C). Measured on 3 October 2026 over a letter-for-letter transcription of every passage ( reading.txt , measure.py ): 1,023 of 1,035 signs read, 98.8%, and 99.9% leaving out the person symbols. The earlier figure of 95% was an estimate. Butler’s wording, pp. 46–59 and 148–151, to be compared with the decipherments here. HathiTrust refuses this project’s automated requests, so the check so far rests on HathiTrust’s page-by-page word counts. The words of every passage deciphered here stand on the matching Butler page (all 17 for f. 58v; a few others are garbled by the OCR of his italics), next to a note on the cypher.

An unsigned cipher letter (BnF fr. 3034 f. 154, DECODE R4223) in Galeazzo Visconti’s invented-sign cipher. George Lasry’s 2023 key, published without a decipherment, was applied and extended on the letter, and 93.3% of the cipher signs give sense. Visconti reports the council of war at Landriano over marching on Milan or Pavia, which he lost; the numbered name codes stay open. ψ me l n y ne ψ … far i l c o n s i … che ne = s · me = l · far = che · 48 = a name Campo a Landriano → the grand maître · invented-sign substitution with numbered codes · 30 August 1528 Galeazzo Visconti to Montmorency from the camp at Landriano, 30 August 1528 to Anne de Montmorency Go to the full text ↓ BnF Français 3034 f. 154r–v, no. 68 (DECODE R4223, catalogue item 177, “unknown sender”). Thirty-nine lines of cipher in Italian. George Lasry published a key for Visconti’s cipher in 2023, with no decipherment of this letter; it was applied here, extended on the letter and checked on two signed sibling letters. 93.3% of the cipher signs give sense; the numbered name codes stay open. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (93% of the cipher) Credits · George Lasry (key or decipherment used) · Satoshi Tomokiyo (identification) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (93% of the cipher) The letter Galeazzo Visconti to Anne de Montmorency, from the camp at Landriano, 30 August 1528: unsigned, two pages, cipher except the opening and close. Where Bibliotèque nationale de France, Français 3034, f. 154r–v (Gallica). DECODE R4223 lists it as “Non-decrypted”, sender unknown. The cipher Each letter is an invented sign, with homophones for vowels and a few signs for syllables, plus numbered code groups for names. How it was read Satoshi Tomokiyo’s cryptiana links the cipher to Visconti, and George Lasry’s 2023 key table gave the letters. The letter itself extended the table. The 39 lines were transcribed sign by sign from Gallica. What it says Visconti describes a council of war on whether the League army should march on Milan or Pavia. He argued for Milan and was interrupted; the army went for Pavia. Still open 1,248 of 1,337 cipher signs give sense (93.3%). Of the 89 unread, 16 are name codes (48, 4θ, 4r, rr, qq, peu ) with no key, the rest one-off signs and blots. Credit Key table: George Lasry; identification of the cipher: Satoshi Tomokiyo.

Français 3034 is a volume of original letters to Montmorency. No. 68, f. 154, opens with three words in clear, Poco scritti le lre , then runs in cipher for thirty lines on the recto and nine on the verso. The close and date are in clear: pregando n[ost]ro S[ign]or Dio dona a V. S. bona e longa vitta. Da al Campo a Landriano ali XXX d’aust . Landriano, south of Milan, was the camp of the League army in the late summer of 1528, after the collapse of Lautrec’s expedition to Naples. f. 154r, lines 1–6: the clear Poco scritti le lre , then “Il consiglio de heri fu per tirare queli capitanei che erano lì a la opinione …”; line 5 ends with the code 48. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3034 f. 154r, via Gallica (view 243). The cipher replaces each letter with an invented sign. The signs include a tau for A, a round d for D, a bold k for R, a psi for I, a sign like ne for S and one like me for L, and a sign written like the word far for CHE. E has three forms and A two. Lasry’s table gave most of the letters. The letter added the values for ne , me , the small y (N, with a bent-arm form for B), θ (G), plain p (M), far and fu , and fixed q as H, or F in Francesco . It also showed that the long thin diagonal strokes under the lines are later word dividers, added by someone who worked on the letter. They are not parts of signs.

Il consiglio de heri fu per tirare queli capitanei che erano lì a la opinione che no fuse andase a Milano, perché era la mia(?) tuto causato comtagio. Scrito questo, s’è chiarito questa mane, ha esendo venuto il duca d’Urbino a casa de [48], per deliberare o a Milano o a Pavia. Ove erano asciilati(?) tuti li capitanei o nostri che [..] sono, molti, et a quesi de la Signoria che sono ascicsai pui(?). [qq] uolse(?) [48] che il duca d’Urbino tirase tuti li so[..] da uno canto et lui li lo[..] da uno altro, aciò dito ognuno sua opinione, lui do[..] deliberaseno [..]. E questa fu inventione de Francesco, dita in secreto ha queli de la Signoria, erano tropo, aciò che se vincese la opinione de andare a Milano. Rex. Il che [..] è [..] parso al duca d’Urbino providitore et maiore parte de loro dal canto nostro. Io era solito sempre esere chiamato il primo per aprire il camino ali altri, et questa volta ha comenciato a Francisco, poi ali altri pochi, poi a me [..] acuvante(?) se; dicese nula, [4θ] dise che ere da andare a Pavia. Io comenciai a dire quelo agio scrito de andare a Milano. Pensate che Francesco il primo a interompere, poi qualche uno altro che mi vergogno dirlo, [4r] sapendolo dissimulare. Rex: il fine mi lasoren[o](?) dire cum fatica, s[e] non(?) fisse. Si va a questo modo se harà uno pastone de mala digestione. Io vedo asai cose, ma che è in mia posa [..] a provederli; e sapiate che tuti li f. 154v nostri, dico tuti, comenciando al capori, [..] e ga[..] Dio ch’io scriva al [peu] et a vostra S. provedase da li che per me ie sono d[..]cuspaeo(?) n[..]ita(?) [..] celaro(?); però mai de dire il servicio dil [peu], e vaglia quanto potrà. Tuta volta certifico em(?) che havem [..] si ne [..] dito il duca d’Urbino providitore, et a io che se andarà per o s[..]u[..]o(?) a traversat[..] il camino tra Milano e Pavia, e don[..]de i ni spire[..]rà(?) poi il resto, [clear] che ca fin de questa ma[teria], pregando n[ost]ro S[ign]or Dio dona a V. S. bona e longa vitta. Da al Campo a Landriano ali XXX d’aust. In English Visconti writes that the council held the day before was meant to bring the captains present round to the view that the army should not go to Milan. That morning the Duke of Urbino came to the lodging of [48] to decide between Milan and Pavia, with all the captains, many of them, and the officers of the Signoria of Venice. It was arranged that each should give his opinion in turn. This, he says, was a device of Francesco’s, whispered to the Venetian officers, so that the vote would go against Milan, and the Duke of Urbino, the proveditor and most of the captains came down against Milan. Visconti was usually called first, “to open the way for the others”. This time Francesco was called first, then a few others, then Visconti. [4θ] said the army should go to Pavia. When Visconti began to argue for Milan, as he had written, Francesco was the first to interrupt, then others he is ashamed to name, and in the end he was let speak only with difficulty. “If it goes on this way we shall have a stew of bad digestion.” He sees much and can do little to remedy it. He asks Montmorency to see to matters for all the captains, in the service of [peu], perhaps the King. The Duke of Urbino and the proveditor have said that the army will go to cut the road between Milan and Pavia, and he will write the rest later. “Francesco” may be Francesco Maria Sforza, the League’s duke of Milan, who wanted Pavia. The letter does not say so.

The two pages are Gallica views 243 and 244 of btv1b90600370. They were deskewed and cut into line strips at full resolution. The line centres drift by up to 90 pixels across the page, so each strip was placed by measurement. A first rough transcription of 1344 tokens showed at once that Lasry’s table gives Italian. Each line was then transcribed again sign by sign against the table, and every value the table lacked was fixed from words already deciphered. A second pass redid the verso and retried every open spot on the recto. Two other Visconti letters in the same cipher were then opened: Visconti to Angelo Bolano, Alessandria, 15 October 1528 (fr. 3045 f. 28), and Visconti to Francis I, in campo in la pieve de Loccate , 15 June 1529 (fr. 3096 f. 91). The key decrypts both (“mal tratamento”, “che disperat-”). In both, the crossed sign appears in numeral pairs, 42 and 48, so it is the figure 4. The name groups of this letter are therefore numbered codes, and 48 appears in the letter to the King as well. The groups rr and qq also recur there as units. None of these codes has a value anywhere.

Re-measured 5 October 2026. 1,248 of 1,337 cipher glyphs read as sense (93.3%). Every open stretch was re-cut from the full-resolution Gallica image and re-read sign by sign; one word was gained ( che havemo , w = O). Lasry’s own table was tested on the open runs (L as a third A, the m-shaped sign as L): no word results. Codes 48 (Saint-Pol?) and peu (the King?) fit every context but none forces the value, so they are not counted. 95% needs 24 more glyphs; 16 of the 89 unread are codes with no key, the rest one-offs and blotted spots. Numbered codes , no key material: 48 (twice; the host of the council), 4θ (the captain who spoke for Pavia), 4r (before sapendolo dissimulare , and again in v03), rr (r21), qq (r09, before uolse ), peu (twice; perhaps the King). Only a surviving nomenclator could fix them. The final sign pair of so··, lo··, do·· (r10–12): the same pair each time. The sense suggests soi , loi , doi , one I value for the pair. That is a proposal only (I). It does not occur in the siblings. One-off signs : [Y r] in r12, a small sign and a blot in r16, [v b] in r30, Π in v08 and v09. The lines make sense without them, so they may be nulls. That is not proved (M). Illegible : only the blotted sign and the flourished ſt ligature in v01. A third pass (22 September 2026) enhanced the other spots on the Gallica native (autocontrast, unsharp mask, threshold, 2×): the middle of v03 is legible, and its ǂ-r pair is the numbered code 4r of r25, so that gap is a code; the r21 rr carries an overbar, so it is the code rr; fuo is Lombard fu , as in the letter to the King. The count is now 1248 of 1337 signs (93.3%). Values decrypted, sense open (M): la mia (r03), asciilati (r07), ascicsai pui (r09), acuvante (r21), lasoreno and se non (r26–27, C), and in v03 and v07 the runs marked (?).

The question was whether the army should march on Milan or on Pavia, and Visconti had argued for Milan. He says a scheme of Francesco's, whispered to the Venetian (Signoria) officers, was meant to swing the vote, and that the Duke of Urbino, the Venetian proveditor and most of the captains then favoured Pavia. Visconti, who was usually asked to speak first, was this time called on after Francesco and the others. When he made the case for Milan he was interrupted, first by Francesco and then by others he is ashamed to name, and in the end he was let speak only with difficulty. He warns that if things go on this way the result will be "a stew of bad digestion". He says he sees much but can do little to remedy it, and asks Montmorency to see to matters for all the captains, in the service of the King (the code "peu"). He reports that the Duke of Urbino and the proveditor have said the army will go to cut the road between Milan and Pavia, and he will write the rest later. Which [..][..][..] is [..] seemed to the Duke of Urbino, the provveditore, and the greater part of them on our side. A radio telegram intercepted at Constantinople and filed unread. A columnar transposition of Russian in Latin letters, 24 columns, key recovered from the ciphertext alone. It is a buying order for hardware for the goods-exchange fund, item by item with sizes. OLDDL VOOSC TNROD TVOTO SAMAD Moscow → Berlin · columnar transposition, 24 columns · 1 June 1921 · key recovered from the ciphertext Voikov to Stomoniakov: nails, rakes and saws from Pyotr Voikov → to Boris Stomoniakov Go to the full text ↓ American officials copied this Soviet radio telegram at Constantinople and could not decipher it. Under a key recovered here it is a shopping list: hardware for trade with the Russian countryside. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 2 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete · On the map ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The telegram Nr 1883/1188/S, signed Voikov, 1 June 1921, Moscow to the Soviet mission in Berlin, for Stomoniakov. Intercepted 7 June. Where NARA RG 59, Central Decimal File 861.00, microfilm M316 roll 42, frame 1273. Part of catalogue 669. The cipher Russian in Latin letters, written in rows of 24 and sent column by column in a secret order. How it was deciphered Annealing against a Russian language model, with no crib. Only width 24 beat shuffled controls, and then the text came out. What it says Buy hardware at once for the goods-exchange fund: iron, nails, shovels, rakes, forks, axes, saws, chisels. Still open A few words in the saw and shovel entries, and where the key came from. No independent reader has checked this yet.
voikov1921.html#the-telegram

The start of the telegram as the Constantinople operator typed it, with its number pair and the word RAION. Image: NARA RG 59, 861.00, M316 roll 42, frame 1273, via the National Archives Catalog. The heading is in clear: Polpred Lutovinov Berlin Delsovpra Stomoniakov , then the numbers 01135–26205 and the word RAION. The same numbers close the text, followed by the date, the serial and the signature. We read the signature as P. L. Voikov and the addressee as B. S. Stomoniakov of the Berlin trade delegation; the frame gives surnames only. The letters are Russian with nothing substituted: across the traffic to Stomoniakov O runs at 11.3%, I at 10.0%, E at 8.8%. So only the order is hidden. Q stands for the soft or hard sign, and punctuation is spelled out: zpt for a comma, dvoetochie for a colon.
voikov1921.html#how-the-key-came-out

The solver tries a column order, reads the rows and scores them against a Russian model. On this model, held-out Russian scores −2.14 per letter and shuffled letters −4.96. At widths 22 to 26, with 120,000 steps, only width 24 stood apart: −4.87 to −5.01 on four restarts, with controls at −5.22 and −5.24. Longer runs at width 24 produced readable Russian (−3.73), and independent restarts gave the same stretches of text in different rotations. After setting Q to the soft sign and moving columns within the row, the score reached −3.21. Read-out order of the columns, 0–23: 5 17 0 23 9 1 16 13 7 18 19 8 12 20 10 6 11 3 21 4 22 2 15 14. A different telegram of the same day carries the same first number, 01135, but this key does not decipher it, so that number does not name the key on its own. The key's source is unknown: its pattern matches nothing in 14 MB of general English or two George Wither texts, the poet Tiltman found behind another Soviet system.
voikov1921.html#what-it-says

For the goods-exchange fund with the countryside it is necessary to buy immediately hardware, colon: tyre iron, horseshoe iron; wire nails from two and a half to seven inches; horseshoe nails of middle sizes; shovels for earthwork, square, nine [or ten] by eleven and three-quarter inches, pointed, ten by eleven and a half inches; rakes; forks for hay and manure; carpenters' axes weighing two and a half to three pounds; cross-cut saws, three and a half, four […] by six inches; joiners' pincers of eight and ten inches; for sharpening saws; mortise chisels up to three-quarters of an inch; flat paring chisels from a half to one and a quarter inches; half-round from a half to one inch. Continuation follows. The Politburo approved "Comrade Kopp's proposal" on 16 April 1921; notes to Lenin's collected works tie it to goods exchange and to Stomoniakov. We have not seen the decision itself, so the link to this order rests on subject matter. The closing prodslid is prod. sled. , the "continuation follows" formula Tiltman quotes from the system he broke on another link.

chetyre shjima : not deciphered; probably a size or unit for the saws. ce before the shovel size: unexplained. de?iatg has a lost letter, so девять or десять. kieszi as клещи (pincers) comes from context, and "for sharpening saws" may be its own item. The letters are autograph notes that Charles VI sent through his Oberststallmeister, outside the Chancellery’s ordinary despatches. The family later copied them into a register (book 5 of inv. 5), numbering them No. 1 to No. 7. No. 1, of 3 February 1720, survives as the autograph (DECODE R5019) and the copy (R5020, pp. 401–404); its cipher is 26 passages, about 190 groups. R5017 is headed Ziffer Schlüssel mit der geheimen Hof-Canzley . It is the deciphering half of a two-part nomenclator. The numbers 1–400 are a scrambled syllabary of letters, bigrams and a few trigrams ( schli , stre , spra ), plus nulls ( errans ), punctuation and the controls annulla praecedentia / sequentia . The numbers 401–977 are words and names in alphabetical order, from Aachen to zu : 458 Cadagan, 513 Duc d’Anjou, 657 Mr. Moroille, 749 D. Orleans, 814 Robethon, 819 Stanhop. In this letter the Emperor writes that “den Ziffer, so ihr mit mir zu brauchen” would follow: the private key R5018, used for the later letters, a different cipher with its own page .

The cipher sits inside the sentences, as in “absonderlich 89 312 251 65 14 312 20 48 96 genau berichten” = den Pentenrider . The autograph and the copy agree group for group. The 26 passages, in order: Register copy, book 5 p. 402: “absonderlich den Pentenrider genau berichten, alles was ihr nur werdt oder geringsten Argwohn machen von Frankreich und dem Regenten ”. Orleans … denke mit dem Duc d’Anjou ein particular Frieden zu machen So the secret instructions are these. Keep Pentenriedter fully informed, confide in the British envoy Cadogan, and show France and the Regent no mistrust. Watch them all the same: now that Alberoni has fallen, France may look for a separate peace with Philip V (whom Vienna still called only “the Duc d’Anjou”) through Morville, the French minister at The Hague. Find out whether Orléans means to make one. Win over the Portuguese envoy and bring his king into the Alliance. On the peace terms, nothing in the Quadruple Alliance treaty is to change: Sardinia for Lorraine is impracticable, the Montferrat equivalent is owed, and the costs of the coming peace must not fall on the Emperor.

Euere schreiben die ihr mir in privato durch mein obristallmeister eingeschickt habt, hab alle nach einander wohl empfangen, wie ihr durch ihn obristallmeister wie auch meine gnädige zufriedenheit werdt vernommen haben; hab aber euch sonders annoch nichts geantwortet, weil theils nur in narrativen bestanden, welches euch hab approbiren lassen, theils ihr durch die gewöhnliche Cantzley rescripta werdt die erleuterung und befehl bekommen haben. Werdt no 2do, wie ich nicht zweifle, werdt ihr mit allen fleiss in guter verstandnuss mit meinen ministren in Frankreich und Engelland stehen, alles ihr vor mein dienst in erfahrung bringt communiciren, wie es auch ihnen befohlen ist; absonderlich [A] genau berichten, alles was ihr nur werdt oder geringsten [B] machen, die aber sondert es mit nöthiger behutsamkeit, absonderlich das ihr gnädig (?) wo ihr glaubt es wohl thun zu können, auch wohl [C], aber auf keine weis [D] bezeigt. Wegen der Tory hat sich nichts verificirt; was aber die ratificacion der convention betrifft, glaub ich werden alle selb nun schon längst ausgewechselt sein und ihr sie also mir durch sichere gelegenheit einschicken könnt. Das aber dessentwegen nicht gleichwohl (absonderlich [E] | [p.403] [F] ist billich anzustehen, also auch nöthig wachtsamb auf seiner hut doch [G] zu sehen. Was die holländische aversion betrifft, werdt ihr das weitere aus den gewöhnlichen rescripten vernemmen. Das gut vernemen und vertrauen [H] ist auf allerweis zu loben; werdt ihr auch ferners so viel möglich continuiren und cultiviren. The cipher carries the substance of the letter: - Windischgrätz is to report everything precisely to **Pentenriedter**. He should speak confidentially with **Cadogan**, the British envoy, and keep Cadogan on side "in every way". Towards **France and the Regent** he must show no suspicion at all. - The Emperor's fear: now that **Alberoni has been expelled from Spain**, **France may seek a separate peace with the Duc d'Anjou** (Philip V, whom Vienna did not recognise as King of Spain) **through Morville**, the French envoy at The Hague. At the end of the letter Windischgrätz is asked to find out whether (as is after all to be believed) **Orléans intends to make a particular peace with d'Anjou**. - **Portugal**: Count Tarouca's good disposition is to be cultivated, with the aim of bringing **his king into the Alliance**. - **The peace terms**: the Emperor will not see **the treaty made between us altered** in the slightest. Giving **Sardinia to the Duke of Lorraine** is "very ideal and hardly feasible". He insists on **the equivalent for Montferrat** and wants the burden of the future peace not to fall on him. Any alteration would wrong **all the allies, even the English themselves**. Euere schreiben die ihr mir in privato durch mein obristallmeister eingeschickt habt, hab alle nach einander wohl empfangen, wie ihr durch ihn obristallmeister wie auch meine gnädige zufriedenheit werdt vernommen haben; hab aber euch sonders annoch nichts geantwortet, weil theils nur in narrativen bestanden, welches euch hab approbiren lassen, theils ihr durch die gewöhnliche Cantzley rescripta werdt die erleuterung und befehl bekommen haben. Nun hab doch nicht unterlassen wollen euch selbst diese Zeylen zu schreiben und euch mein zufriedenheit über euren eyfer und bis itzt sowohl zu Hanover als in Haag geleistete aufführung zu bezeigen, wie auch das mir euere geheimb brief angenemb, ihr auch mit selben continuiren sollt, absonderlich wo was geheimeres oder wo ihr ein anstoss oder anfrag über die cantzley rescripta oder sonst in wichtigen negocys es nötig finden soltet. Nun nur auf einige principaliora zu antworten, schicke euch hiemit (so er noch fertig) oder mit negster gelegenheit den Ziffer, so ihr mit mir zu brauchen, dieweil der (?) der Hof cantzley kont dienen. Werdt no 2do, wie ich nicht zweifle, werdt ihr mit allen fleiss in guter verstandnuss mit meinen ministren in Frankreich und Engelland stehen, alles ihr vor mein dienst in erfahrung bringt communiciren, wie es auch ihnen befohlen ist; absonderlich ⟦den Pentenrider⟧ genau berichten, alles was ihr nur werdt oder geringsten ⟦Argwon machen von Frankreich undt dem Regenten⟧, die aber sondert es mit nöthiger behutsamkeit, absonderlich das ihr gnädig (?) wo ihr glaubt es wohl thun zu können, auch wohl ⟦mit dem Cadagan cunfident erofnet⟧, aber auf keine weis ⟦gegen dem Frankreich auch kein geringstn Argwon⟧ bezeigt. Wegen der Tory hat sich nichts verificirt; was aber die ratificacion der convention betrifft, glaub ich werden alle selb nun schon längst ausgewechselt sein und ihr sie also mir durch sichere gelegenheit einschicken könnt. Das aber dessentwegen nicht gleichwohl (absonderlich ⟦da nun der Alberoni aus Spannien abgeschaft⟧ ⟦[zu] fichten, das Frankreich vielleicht suche mit Duc d'Anjou ein sonder Frieden zum Mr. Morville⟧) ist billich anzustehen, also auch nöthig wachtsamb auf seiner hut doch ⟦ohne [?ein]ichn geringsten Argwon⟧ zu sehen. Was die holländische aversion betrifft, werdt ihr das weitere aus den gewöhnlichen rescripten vernemmen. Das gut vernemen und vertrauen ⟦mit dem Graf Daroqui⟧ ist auf allerweis zu loben; werdt ihr auch ferners so viel möglich continuiren und cultiviren. Finden wir ohne dem schon ⟦von Portugal aus⟧ sein gute neigung, bedankt ihr ihm auch desswegen, ein gnädige expression werdt machen können; könnt ihr auch sagen das 50 (?) verdriesst ⟦seyn König mir der Allianz⟧ und den ⟦publico kein mehreren darum⟧ thun könnt als seinen ⟦König in die Allianz⟧ zu bringen, auf welches auch sich auf allerweis zu verrichten wegen eigener schildung (?), aber werdt weiters bedacht sein, dan es noch nicht de tempore; auf das obige aber mich ⟦Portugal denken⟧; das wird nicht wohl ⟦seyn emesuren nimbt undt Beytritt [446] ein von Spanien untertructt⟧ werden können. Die gern in Ziffer mir überschreibene wegnissten (?) seindt mir gar lieb und werdt ihr also mit allen fleiss und aufmerksamkeit continuiren. Was die rest betrifft ist es zu erwarten und auf seiner hut zu stehen, und werdt ihr ⟦Cadagan⟧ auf all weis suchen beyzuhalten, auch ihr bedeuten wie mich auf ihn und sein eyfer vor die gemein auch gantz verlasse, auch ihn danken und die unbilligkeit so wohl als schaden ⟦aller alliirten, ia Engelländer selbst⟧ zu erkennen geben. Man ⟦in künfften Frieden⟧ nur das geringste wider ⟦die zwischen uns gemachte Tractat geendert würde⟧; das under wegen ⟦Sardinien dem Herzog von Lothringen⟧ zu geben ist sehr ideal und nicht wohl thunlich; endlich auch ⟦wie der dem quten glauben der Tractat⟧, also nicht wohl darauf zu denken, das sonst ⟦mir das aequivalent von monferat⟧ höchst beschwerlich ist, nicht ohne wan auch höchst billich auch dahin anzutragen, das in ⟦künfften Frieden⟧ dieses onus nicht auf mich fall, sondern wo möglich die den ⟦dem Duc d'Anjou⟧ oder dem so ⟦gross [zu] [638] dem nutz⟧ excindirt werde. Das übrig werdt ihr sonst vernemen, und hab mir sonst nichts bey euch zu erinnern, als das ihr mit euren fleiss und application continuirt, mir alle genau nachricht zu geben, absonderlich recht zu sehen ob (wie wohl endlich zu glauben) ⟦D. Orleans⟧ denke ⟦mit dem Duc d'Anjou ein particular Frieden [zu] machen⟧; und das mit eurer aufführung annoch gnädigst wohl zufrieden bin, wie dan euer gnädigster herr verbleibe. Carl. Wien den 3. febr. 1720. Your letters, which you sent me privately through my Master of the Horse, I have all received safely one after the other, as you will have learned through him, the Master of the Horse, as also my gracious satisfaction; but I have not yet answered you particularly, because they consisted partly only of narratives, which I have had approved for you, and partly you will have received the explanation and orders through the usual chancery rescripts. Now I have nevertheless not wished to omit writing these lines to you myself, and to show you my satisfaction with your zeal and with the conduct you have shown up to now both at Hanover and at The Hague, as also that your secret letters are welcome to me, and that you are to continue with them, especially where there is something more secret, or where you should find it necessary on some difficulty or query about the chancery rescripts, or otherwise in important business. Now, to answer only some principal points: I send you herewith (if it is ready) or by the next opportunity the cipher which you are to use with me, since the (?) of the Court Chancery could serve. Secondly, as I do not doubt, you will with all diligence stay in good understanding with my ministers in France and England, and communicate to them all you learn for my service, as they have also been ordered; especially report precisely to ⟦Pentenriedter⟧ everything that you only will or the least ⟦suspicion make of France and the Regent⟧, which however set it apart with the necessary caution; especially that you, graciously (?), where you believe you can well do it, also ⟦open yourself confidentially to Cadogan⟧, but in no way show ⟦towards France the least suspicion either⟧. Concerning the Tories nothing has been verified; but as for the ratification of the convention, I believe they will all long since have been exchanged, and you can send them to me by a safe opportunity. That nevertheless on that account not (especially ⟦now that Alberoni has been expelled from Spain⟧, ⟦[to] fear that France may perhaps seek a separate peace with the Duc d'Anjou through Monsieur Morville⟧) is fit to be considered, and so it is also necessary to be watchful on one's guard, yet ⟦without the least suspicion⟧ to look on. As for the Dutch aversion, you will learn the rest from the usual rescripts. The good understanding and confidence ⟦with Count Tarouca⟧ is to be praised in every way; you will also continue and cultivate it further as far as possible. We already find without that ⟦from Portugal⟧ his good inclination; thank him for it too; you will be able to make a gracious expression; you can also say that 50 (?) it vexes ⟦his King me the Alliance⟧ and the ⟦publico no more about it⟧ you could do than to bring his ⟦King into the Alliance⟧, on which also to proceed in every way because of his own description (?), but you will be further mindful, for it is not yet the time; but on the above, ⟦think of Portugal⟧ for me; that will not well ⟦be, measures [?ere] it takes, and accession [446] one of Spain suppressed⟧ can be. The news (?) gladly sent me in cipher are very dear to me, and so you will continue with all diligence and attention. As for the rest, it is to be awaited and to be on one's guard; and you will seek in every way to keep ⟦Cadogan⟧ on side, and let him know how I rely entirely on him and his zeal for the common cause, and thank him, and make known the injustice as well as the harm ⟦to all the allies, yes, to the English themselves⟧, if one ⟦in the future peace⟧ in the least against ⟦the treaty made between us should be altered⟧; that giving ⟦Sardinia to the Duke of Lorraine⟧ in the meantime is very ideal and not well feasible; finally also ⟦as the [?] to the good faith of the treaty⟧, so it is not well to be thought of, that otherwise ⟦the equivalent of Montferrat for me⟧ is most burdensome, not without, if also most just, to press for this too, that in ⟦the future peace⟧ this burden should not fall on me, but, where possible, be cut off for the ⟦Duc d'Anjou⟧ or for him so ⟦great [to] [638] the benefit⟧. The rest you will learn otherwise, and I have nothing else to remind you of, except that you continue with your diligence and application to give me all exact news, especially to see rightly whether (as is after all to be believed) ⟦the Duc d'Orléans⟧ thinks ⟦of making a particular peace with the Duc d'Anjou⟧; and that I am still most graciously well satisfied with your conduct, as I remain your most gracious lord. Charles. Vienna, 3 February 1720. Key: key5017_syllabary.tsv , key5017_nomenclator.tsv
